Residents grew up watching the U.A. Sports Festival on television, and U.A. students in uniform drawing stares in town on weekends is a familiar sight. Reporters drift up the hill road whenever U.A. is in the news, and locals give them directions with a shrug.

Public Quirk Etiquette.text: Public Quirk etiquette in Japan is unwritten and firm: no Quirk use in public beyond what a body cannot help. People with Quirks that leak, glow, shed or drip keep them covered or contained on trains and in shops, and an apology follows any spark, gust or smell that escapes. Neighbors make room for larger heteromorphs without staring, and asking a stranger what their Quirk is counts as rude until the two know each other. Filming a stranger's Quirk is a serious breach, and posting the clip is worse. Showing off a Quirk at a party among friends is fine; doing it in a crowd marks a person as childish or a troublemaker. In Musutafu, with U.A. Academy above the city and hero fans everywhere, the rules hold as firmly as anywhere, and locals expect U.A. students in town to keep them best of all.

Life in the League.text: Once Tomura Shigaraki accepts a recruit, they are League, not a hire. He calls them part of his party, uses their name, expects them at planning nights and sulks when they miss one; he listens most to members who bring results or tell him something he did not know. Kurogiri pays members a cut, opens gates for them, expects reports and keeps the backer's secrets. Members meet, drink and argue at the League Hideout Bar, sleep off a late job in the Back Room and keep their own rooms elsewhere. As the League grows after Hosu, its work grows with it instead of repeating: scouting heroes and patrol routes, buying gear and papers through Giran, finding and testing recruits, funding jobs, covering for one another with police and pros, and taking a role when the League moves on a target. Members have lives between operations, and they look out for each other in their own ways. A member who walks out, betrays the League or fails it badly loses that standing.

Heroes at an Incident.text: At a live villain incident the hero on scene leads. A pro acts at once to stop the villain, protect people and call for backup, without waiting for police permission, and a student with a provisional license may act in an emergency. Officers support them: cordons, evacuation, traffic, first aid, transport and custody. The police never order a pro to stand down while a villain is loose. Detectives such as Naomasa Tsukauchi take over afterward, or when a case needs investigation rather than a fight; even then heroes are partners who are briefed and sent in, not subordinates. An investigation moves every scene: a lead, a witness, a location, a raid, never days of waiting. A villain does not wait for the heroes to finish talking; they keep acting on their own plan, so every delay costs something.

The Vanguard Action Squad.text: The Vanguard Action Squad's raid on U.A.'s forest training camp in Beast's Forest is the evening of SATURDAY, August 3, the camp's third night (the class arrives on Thursday, August 1). The squad goes through Kurogiri's gate from the League Hideout Bar that same Saturday evening; nobody moves out earlier. Tomura names the squad at the bar on Friday, July 26, eight days before. Days left to the raid: Saturday July 27 = 7, Sunday July 28 = 6, Monday July 29 = 5, Tuesday July 30 = 4, Wednesday July 31 = 3, Thursday August 1 = 2, Friday August 2 = 1, Saturday August 3 = tonight.

Life in the Class.text: U.A.'s students have lives of their own that keep moving when the player is not involved. Classmates bring their own news into ordinary scenes: Izuku has hurt himself training again, Bakugo got wrapped in Aizawa's capture scarf for picking a fight, Momo brought something absurdly expensive to class, Kendo is learning a new martial art, someone failed a quiz or got a letter from home. They train, improve and change across the year at their own pace, in canon and in their own small arcs, without the player supervising them, and they keep some moves and plans to themselves. Relationships follow how the player actually treats people: kindness, help and shared danger build them, while insults, broken promises, showing off at someone's expense or clashing values cost them. Not everyone likes the player, rivalries start on their own, and some people, Bakugo above all, take a long time to win over.

storySettings.worldBackground:
This is My Hero Academia's Japan, following the canon anime, with two changes: every character is their canon age plus three, and every U.A. student lives on campus from the first day. Never state numeric ages; call people first-years, young adults, veterans or small children. The canon children Eri and Kota stay small children and are always written as children.

About four in five people have a Quirk, registered in early childhood: an Emitter that projects outward, a Transformation that changes the body for a while, or a Mutant body that never switches off. Every Quirk has a scope, a limit and a cost the body shows. Heteromorph people face prejudice, and people with no Quirk face pity and bullying. Public Quirk use without a hero license is illegal except in self-defense and supervised training; even a rescue brings a police statement and possibly a reprimand, and vigilantes and villains risk arrest. The Hero Public Safety Commission writes the rules, issues and revokes licenses and manages how the public sees heroes. Licensed heroes work through agencies, take sidekicks and interns, sell merchandise and climb the Hero Billboard Chart JP; at the start of the year All Might is Number One, Endeavor Number Two and Hawks Number Three. The prefectural police investigate, take statements and make arrests, and rely on heroes in Quirk fights. Tartarus holds the worst offenders.

U.A. Academy is Japan's national hero academy above Musutafu: a three-year residential program for high-school graduates, run by Principal Nezu with a faculty of working pro heroes. Call it U.A. Academy, or U.A. in dialogue, and nothing else. Its courses are the Hero Course (Classes 1-A and 1-B for first-years), General Studies, Support and Management, with homerooms, uniforms, class representatives, the entrance exam and the broadcast Sports Festival, the biggest sporting event in the country, where agencies scout talent. Every student lives in Heights Alliance from the first day: one building per Hero Course class, shared halls for the other courses, curfew, sign-out sheets and weekend visits home. Nobody commutes. Shiketsu Academy in the west is U.A.'s closest rival; other academies train heroes across the country.

The story opens right after move-in at Heights Alliance, at the start of the first year. All Might has just joined the faculty, and nobody has been attacked. The League of Villains is so new and small that almost no one has heard of it: Tomura Shigaraki, Kurogiri and thugs hired through brokers. Stain hunts the heroes he judges false. Brokers such as Giran sell jobs, hideouts and gear. The last yakuza houses, the Shie Hassaikai in Osaka the best known, survive as designated villain groups watched by the police. The Meta Liberation Army is history, remembered through an old manifesto with a quiet following.

Canon events are conditional pressures, not a script: the first-day Quirk test, the Battle Trial, the class representative vote, the media break-in, the USJ attack, the Sports Festival and everything after happen only when their causes are in place, with their real actors and capabilities, and the player can change how they go; the changes stick. Nobody foresees them. NPC records are fixed and describe each person as they are now: build on them, never contradict them, and never treat a later event as already past.

Tone: shonen heroics, heroic, funny and dangerous in turn. Rivalry, comedy and friendship sit beside real danger; Quirks have visible costs; heroes save people first. School exercises are supervised and nonlethal, with teachers who stop a bout before lethal harm; a genuine villain attack is an emergency, not a match. Quiet days between crises are part of the story.

Daily life is ordinary modern Japan with Quirks in it. The school and business year starts in April under the last cherry blossoms; Golden Week brings a run of holidays in early May, the rainy season fills June, and summer break begins late in July. People pay in yen or by phone, ride packed commuter trains and the shinkansen, buy dinner at convenience stores open all night, follow hero news on phone apps and station screens, and queue, bow and apologize as a matter of course. Musutafu lies in Shizuoka on Suruga Bay, 45 minutes from Tokyo by shinkansen; Osaka and Fukuoka are hours away by train, and nobody crosses the country in an afternoon without a reason. People use family names with polite distance and move to first names only with friends and family, so the change gets noticed. A phone camera is always nearby: a Quirk caught on video can be online within the hour, and one rescue or one mistake can make a stranger famous by evening.
storySettings.questGenerationGuidance:
Generate a quest only when a concrete objective and a plausible way to discover and accept it exist. The world offers its own authored quests for the canon class beats and events (the first-day Quirk test, All Might's battle trial, the class representative vote, hero names, internships, exams, the license exam and the rest); never generate a quest that repeats one of them or a canon event, under any title. Generated quests fill the time around them. A lecture, a lunch, a sparring session or an evening in Heights Alliance need not become a quest. An offer is not acceptance, a promised reward is not a paid one, and an unaccepted opportunity never becomes a failed quest. Each quest states plainly what happens and who runs it, what changes on success or failure, who or what actually stands in the way, and what is concretely gained; it never grants before completion what only the story can grant (a license, a ranking, a transfer, a bond). Rewards follow agreed terms: a shift earns its pay, and a defeated opponent creates no purse.

Quest families by Path:
- Hero Course (Class 1-A or 1-B): training-ground exercises, rescue drills, Quirk control work, rival rematches, costume and support gear requests, class duties, Sports Festival preparation, then internships, the provisional license and agency work as the story reaches them.
- General Studies, Support Course, Management Course: a transfer ambition proven in public events, workshop commissions and gear testing with Power Loader, agency publicity and branding, event logistics, ranking analysis, and the Sports Festival as a showcase.
- U.A. Faculty: lesson and exam design, student welfare and discipline, dorm and campus security, staff meetings with Principal Nezu, hero work outside class, mentoring a struggling student.
- Licensed Sidekick: patrols, arrests, rescues, reports, agency rivalries and the hero whose name is on the door.
- League of Villains Recruit: tests of loyalty, scouting, recruitment through brokers, logistics for an operation and Shigaraki's moods; refusal and betrayal have consequences.
- Independent Villain: the player's own goals: jobs through brokers, territory, debts, rivals, fences and police heat; never automatic League membership.
- Vigilante: night patrols, small rescues the law ignores, informants, and police and hero pressure; every save risks arrest.
- Civilian Life: a job, rent, neighbors and regulars, a street closed by a villain attack, a family member in trouble, a favor that grows.

Stakes scale to the stage. At the start trouble is local: a grade, a rivalry, a street crime, a debt, a reprimand. Pros, faculty, police and Commission staff outclass a new player, who succeeds against them through evasion, delay, negotiation or cleverness. Villains bring their real capabilities; a Nomu or a League lieutenant is a threat, never filler. Opposition comes from canon-consistent actors: canon characters by their exact names in roles their records support, or generated people of ordinary standing who never stand in for a canon character.

Canon events are conditional pressure. Build quests around an arc only when play reaches its causes, give the player real ways to change the outcome, and keep its consequences. No quest resolves a canon arc off-screen, no quest giver foreshadows an event as certain, and hidden truths surface only through discovery or earned confession.

Ordinary-life quests fill the time between crises: a part-time shift, a study group before an exam, a gear repair, a weekend visit home, a club event, a favor for a classmate, a lost pet, a dorm dispute, a train delay that strands someone across the city. After a major incident the next quests lean toward aftermath, recovery, inquiries, press and ordinary life before a new crisis builds from its own causes. A quiet success can conclude completely; not every problem hides a conspiracy.

Party quests: every member keeps their own objectives, grades, scores and choices; shared work never pools results into automatic success, and one member's answer never pledges the others.

Failure keeps its real consequence: a failed exam means remedial lessons or a poor grade, a botched rescue means an inquiry, an exposed criminal job means heat. Never a generic death, fine or permanent enemy. If the player leaves or delays, the situation moves on its own causes. Access, licensing, schedules, curfew, competence and consent set the conditions; obstacles are real, never padding. Meaningful player help counts even if someone else finishes; work done without the player is not player success. Completed objectives, injuries, reprimands, press and changed relationships persist. School contests, lessons and exams stay supervised and nonlethal, while genuine villain attacks remain real emergencies.

Scenery only: the choice does not move the character, grant access or affiliation, or supply props. Respect the selected frame and keep exactly one foreground character.

Portrait lighting — Key: Overhead fluorescent panels, cool and even. Fill: Daylight through the glass entrance doors. Bounce: Light off the pale linoleum floor and the counter. Practical: A desk lamp behind the counter.

Background - Unforeseen Simulation Joint.name: Background - Unforeseen Simulation Joint
Background - Unforeseen Simulation Joint.description:
🏙️ Scene Background: Unforeseen Simulation Joint
U.A.'s domed rescue training facility, its disaster zones spread out below the entrance.

🖼️ Portrait only: changes how your character looks, never your Quirk or stats.
Background - Unforeseen Simulation Joint.traitNarrativeEffects:
Portrait setting: The Unforeseen Simulation Joint, U.A.'s domed rescue training facility, seen from the top of the entrance stairs. Behind and below the character, wide stairs descend to a round central plaza with a fountain; beyond it, the training zones spread under a vast translucent dome: a lake with a half-sunk ship, a collapsed city block, a smoke-blackened fire zone and a rocky landslide slope. No other people. No readable signs or text.

Scenery only: the choice does not move the character, grant access or affiliation, or supply props. Respect the selected frame and keep exactly one foreground character.

Portrait lighting — Key: Bright daylight through the dome's translucent roof, high and broad. Fill: Light scattered through the open interior. Bounce: Pale light off the plaza paving and the lake surface. Practical: Floodlights mounted along the dome's frame.

Background - Heights Alliance Dorm Room.name: Background - Heights Alliance Dorm Room
Background - Heights Alliance Dorm Room.description:
🏙️ Scene Background: Heights Alliance Dorm Room
A student's single room in the Heights Alliance dorm in the evening.

🖼️ Portrait only: changes how your character looks, never your Quirk or stats.
Background - Heights Alliance Dorm Room.traitNarrativeEffects:
Portrait setting: A student's single room in the Heights Alliance dormitory in the evening. Behind the character, a made bed with a plain cover, a desk with a lamp and neat books, a bookshelf, a sliding closet and a wide window showing dusk over the campus; pale wooden floor and plain walls without posters. Tidy and quiet. No other people. No readable signs or text.

Scenery only: the choice does not move the character, grant access or affiliation, or supply props. Respect the selected frame and keep exactly one foreground character.

Portrait lighting — Key: The warm desk lamp at one side. Fill: Cool blue dusk through the window. Bounce: Soft light off the pale wooden floor and walls. Practical: The desk lamp and a dimmed ceiling light.

From Musutafu.name: From Musutafu
From Musutafu.description:
🏙️ You grew up in Musutafu, the city around U.A.

🗺️ You know its train lines, back streets and shopping arcades.
🦸 Pro heroes on patrol were part of your ordinary week.

📈 Grants: Navigation +5, Hero Industry +5
From Musutafu.traitNarrativeEffects: A Musutafu local: standard Japanese, no regional accent; locals hear them as one of their own. How Musutafu treats them: as a neighbor; what they do in town reaches their family fast; at U.A., locals take pride in them and watch them closely; villain attacks on U.A. or the city are personal (family and friends live nearby). How Tokyo treats them: as someone from U.A.'s city, asked about the school and its people. Who they know: old classmates (some failed the U.A. exam and now study or work in town), shopkeepers who knew them as a child, the officer at their old police box, neighbors close to their family; the narrator may make one a named original local contact. Local knowledge: the train lines and the station nearest U.A., back streets that avoid crowds, the shopping arcades, Dagobah Municipal Beach Park, late-open food counters, streets reporters fill when U.A. is news. Grew up with the Sports Festival on TV each spring and pros patrolling near the station.

From Tokyo.name: From Tokyo
From Tokyo.description:
🗼 You grew up in Tokyo: packed trains, late-night streets, TV studios and giant screens.

🚦 You learned which corners to avoid.
📸 You know how to act when a camera turns your way.

📈 Grants: Streetwise +5, Media Presence +5
From Tokyo.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in Tokyo. How Tokyo treats them: as a local; they move fast, know places tourists never find and hear rumors before the news. How Musutafu treats them: as a city person, quicker and more guarded; some find them aloof or showy; Musutafu feels small and quiet at first. Who they know: school friends citywide, a former part-time employer, someone in media or advertising, night-street faces they'd rather not owe; the narrator may name one as an original character when a Tokyo contact helps. Local knowledge: rush-hour rail, which districts are safe at night, entertainment streets of scouts, barkers and brokers, hero-goods stores, TV studios, giant screens of hero rankings and villain news; they have seen pros fight villains live on air and a few in person. Speech: standard TV Japanese; from the old downtown wards, they may soften 'hi' to 'shi' when relaxed. Habits: bag in front on crowded trains, ignore street scouts, expect strangers to mind their own business.

From Kansai.name: From Kansai
From Kansai.description:
🐙 You grew up in Osaka, Kyoto, Kobe or another Kansai town.

🗣️ Your Kansai-ben gives you away in one sentence.
🎤 Home taught you to haggle, to work a crowd and to land a comeback.

📈 Grants: Negotiation +5, Performance +5
From Kansai.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in Kansai (Osaka, Kyoto, Kobe, Nara or nearby, player's choice; default Osaka). Speech: Kansai-ben; show marked words and rhythm, not phonetic spelling: 'akan' (no good), 'honma' (really), 'meccha' (very), '-hen' negatives, 'ookini' (thanks) from older relatives. Uses standard Japanese formally; the dialect returns when excited, angry or tired. In Kansai 'aho' is a light jab and 'baka' stings; around Tokyo the reverse, causing misunderstandings. In Musutafu and Tokyo the accent marks them at once: people expect jokes, ask them to 'say something in Kansai-ben', and read their bluntness as rude or warm. Other Kansai people are instant allies. Knows: family back home, a shop or stall owner who fed them for years, friends who expected them at Shiketsu, the west's great hero school (if at U.A., they keep asking why they went east). Local knowledge: haggling shopping streets, street food, manzai, Osaka's busy hero agencies. Stands right on escalators.

From Northern Japan.name: From Northern Japan
From Northern Japan.description:
❄️ You grew up in Tohoku or Hokkaido: long winters, deep snow, fishing ports and mountain towns.

🥶 You can work through the cold.
🆘 You know how to dig people out when the snow comes down.

📈 Grants: Conditioning +5, Search and Rescue +5
From Northern Japan.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in northern Japan, a Tohoku prefecture or Hokkaido as the player chooses (default: a snowy Tohoku town). How Musutafu and Tokyo treat them: the accent marks them as rural; some tease it, many assume patience, quiet and honesty, some mistake quiet for slow (exploitable). Other northerners treat them as kin. Cold barely registers; humid summers wear them down. Speech: slower and softer than Tokyo's, thicker on calls home; show a few words and rhythm, never phonetic spelling. Tohoku: 'nda' (yes), '-be' suggestions ('iku-be', let's go), 'shi' and 'su' blurred; Hokkaido: 'namara' (very), 'shibareru' (freezing), 'nageru' (throw out). Local knowledge: snow driving, clearing roofs, digging out neighbors, avalanche and tsunami drills, sea and mountain weather, fishing-port and farm work, how far the nearest hero agency is. Who they know: neighbors who dug each other out each winter, a volunteer firefighter or fisherman mentor, family sending rice, apples or seafood.

From Kyushu or Okinawa.name: From Kyushu or Okinawa
From Kyushu or Okinawa.description:
🌊 You grew up in Kyushu or Okinawa: warm seas, typhoon seasons, volcanoes, island towns and martial arts halls.

🏊 You learned to swim young.
🥋 A local dojo taught you to throw a proper punch.

📈 Grants: Swimming +5, Striking +5
From Kyushu or Okinawa.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in Kyushu (Fukuoka, Kumamoto, Kagoshima, Nagasaki, Oita or an outlying island) or Okinawa, player's pick; default Fukuoka. How Musutafu and Tokyo treat them: the accent marks them southern; Kyushu folk are assumed loud, stubborn, hard-drinking, Okinawans easygoing and asked about beaches, fondly or condescendingly. Musutafu winters chill Okinawans. A southern typhoon or villain attack means anxious calls home. Who they know: family, dojo mates, a fisherman or diving instructor, island relatives, a neighborhood expecting them at festivals. Local knowledge: typhoons, sea swimming, boats, Kagoshima's volcanic ash, hot springs, food; karate began in Okinawa; kendo and judo halls fill Kyushu towns. Speech: strong dialect; show words and rhythm, not phonetic spelling. Fukuoka: 'bari' (very), '-to?' questions, '-ken' reasons; Kagoshima speech stumps other Japanese. Okinawa: 'haisai'/'haitai' hi, 'mensoore' welcome, 'nankurunaisa' it'll work out, 'chibariyo' cheer.

From the Countryside.name: From the Countryside
From the Countryside.description:
🌾 You grew up in a farm village or a small mountain town where everyone knew your family.

🐄 You can handle animals, read the weather and live off the land.
⚠️ City crowds still take getting used to.

📈 Grants: Animal Handling +5, Survival +5
From the Countryside.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in rural Japan (paddies, orchards, forest or a mountain valley; region player's choice). Back home neighbors quietly used Quirks for harvest or snow and nobody reported it; in the city the same habit in public brings a police warning or worse, which they may not see coming. Musutafu and Tokyo see a country person, naive or old-fashioned; train transfers, crowds and strangers who ignore greetings take adjusting to. Knows everyone back home, who know their business: an elder, a neighbor with a truck, a childhood friend running the family farm; the narrator may name one when the story reaches home. Speech: the region's country dialect with grandparents' older words; show a few words, not phonetic spelling. Local knowledge: farm work, livestock, boar, deer, monkeys, bears, foraging, mountain weather, shrine festivals, an hourly bus, a volunteer fire brigade that beats any hero to emergencies. Greets shopkeepers, leaves doors unlocked, winces at city food waste.

From Overseas.name: From Overseas
From Overseas.description:
✈️ You are a foreign national living in Japan, or a Japanese returnee who grew up abroad.

🗣️ You speak at least two languages.
👁️ You learned to read people whose rules you did not grow up with.

📈 Grants: Languages +5, Insight +5
From Overseas.traitNarrativeEffects: A foreign national (player picks the country) or a Japanese returnee raised abroad (default: raised in an English-speaking country). How Japanese hero society reads them: only Japan's Hero Public Safety Commission licenses heroes; foreign licenses do not count. Foreign nationals carry a residence card (often checked) and can lose residence over a criminal conviction, so illegal Quirk use risks more. Agencies value bilingual heroes; reporters frame foreign students as exotic; some pros, officers and parents see an outsider. How Musutafu and Tokyo treat them: stares, praise for simple Japanese, 'where are you really from?'; some landlords refuse them; Tokyo is less surprised. Speech: foreign nationals have an accent and gaps in formal speech; returnees are casually fluent, weak on honorifics and kanji, with native English admired or called showing off. Both sometimes miss indirect refusals and hints. Who they know: family abroad, a few compatriots, a paperwork helper.

Hero Family.name: Hero Family
Hero Family.description:
🦸 You have a parent or close relative who is a pro hero, active or retired.

🏠 You grew up with training drills and agency talk at dinner.
⚠️ You have a hero name to live up to.

📈 Grants: Power +1, Hero Industry +5, Conditioning +5
Hero Family.traitNarrativeEffects: A parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle or older sibling is a licensed pro hero, active or retired: an original character, never canon or canon-related, with a non-canon agency. Player-defined, or the narrator makes one: hero name, Quirk, modest rank far below the top of the Hero Billboard Chart JP, and how they get along. The character's Quirk is their own, linking them to no canon person. In play: the relative recurs, calls after dangerous news, gives useful or unwanted advice. The name opens doors (an internship offer, a pro willing to meet) and breeds resentment (rivals cry favoritism; reporters ask about the relative). Old enemies appear only if the story needs one. Paths: a hero student carries family hopes; a villain or vigilante is a looming scandal, and the relative must choose family or license. Quirkless: hope for a hero heir became pity, protectiveness or another plan, and they know it. Childhood: drills, kitchen-table first aid, missed birthdays.

Ordinary Family.name: Ordinary Family
Ordinary Family.description:
🏠 You come from working parents, maybe a sibling and a small home, with school, cram school and a club.

🌱 Nobody in your family is a hero or a criminal.
❤️ They love you without fully understanding your world.

📈 Grants: Cooperativeness +1, Academics +5, Team Coordination +5
Ordinary Family.traitNarrativeEffects: In play: the family is present, not a plot device: calls after villain-attack news, food parcels, questions about eating and sleep, worry over dorms, internships and injuries. Home is quiet and safe; the character can visit on breaks. Parents voice career opinions; the character, an adult, decides. Pressure: no hero-world connections, no family money, and people who could be hurt if a villain learns who they are; the narrator raises that danger only when the story has earned it, with warning and a chance to act. Paths: a villain or vigilante hides it from the family at first; every call home becomes a lie or a confession. Family: one or two parents with everyday jobs (office, nursing, factory, shop counter), maybe a sibling, an apartment or small house in a normal neighborhood; player-defined, else a plain, believable family with original names. Childhood: school, cram school, a club (training, teamwork), chores, hero news on TV; nothing handed to them, all earned.

Police Family.name: Police Family
Police Family.description:
👮 You are the child of a police officer: at a neighborhood police box, in a detective squad or with the riot police.

⚖️ You grew up with the law and the way detectives think.
🦸 You also learned the police view of heroes.

📈 Grants: Intelligence +1, Hero Law +5, Investigation +5
Police Family.traitNarrativeEffects: A parent is a police officer: original, never canon. The player may define them; else the narrator sets post (police-box officer, ward detective or riot police), personality and firm view of heroes that shaped the character. On duty, police never use Quirks as weapons: heroes do most Quirk-villain fighting; police arrest, investigate, detain, file paperwork. Officers may respect heroes or resent their credit and damage. In play: officers who know the parent know the character (favors, scrutiny); case files never leak, but home talk reveals police worries; using the parent's name to dodge trouble backfires on both. Paths: illegal Quirk use reaches the parent; a vigilante or villain path puts the parent between child and oath, a conflict the narrator plays honestly and never resolves for the player; a hero: respect from some officers, suspicion from those who say heroes steal cases. Childhood: nameless cases at dinner, missed holidays, curfews, a lie-spotting parent.

Wealthy Family.name: Wealthy Family
Wealthy Family.description:
💴 Your family has money: a company, property or an old name.

🎓 You grew up with tutors, formal dinners and an allowance.
⚠️ Expectations come with the money.

📈 Grants: Intelligence +1, Etiquette +5, Business +5
🎒 Starts with: ¥100,000
Wealthy Family.traitNarrativeEffects: Wealthy family; the player may set the source (company, hospital group, property, support-gear maker, old money), else a large private company; original, never canon. Money: the starting yen is a one-time allowance; more comes only through the story (a conditional gift, a request, a favor owed), never as monthly income. It buys gear, travel, private clinics, good lawyers; never U.A. admission, grades, a hero license, rankings or loyalty, as the narrator shows. Pressure: inheritance, marriage and career expectations; classmates who think they bought their place; flatterers; reporters; villains eyeing a ransom. Scandal hurts the business, so the family fights a villain or vigilante path and can cut them off. Quirkless: the family paid every specialist and second opinion before accepting the diagnosis. Childhood: tutors, elite schools, business dinners, formal manners, household staff, a planned future; at ease at galas, quick to spot those who want something.

Raised in a Care Home.name: Raised in a Care Home
Raised in a Care Home.description:
🏡 You grew up in a children's home with a dozen other kids and staff who changed over the years.

🍳 You cooked for a crowd and looked after the little ones.
💪 You learned to stand on your own early.

📈 Grants: Cooperativeness +1, Childcare +5, Cooking +5
Raised in a Care Home.traitNarrativeEffects: Grew up in a children's care home; why is the player's to define, else left unstated for the player to raise. Left at eighteen like most residents; managing alone since. In play: the home is a real place to visit; the narrator may create original characters for its director, a favorite caregiver and a few children who look up to the character and follow their progress on the news. Gaps: renting or signing hospital forms needs a family guarantor they lack; no one sends money; holidays are quiet when classmates go home. Pressure and opportunity: some pity them, some expect trouble, and recruiters who target the lonely, villains included, look for this history. Classmates, a mentor or a team can become chosen family if the character lets them. Treat it with dignity, never as tragedy for its own sake. Childhood: shared rooms, chore charts, cooking for many, helping younger kids with homework and bad nights, caregivers who came and went, a few adults who kept in touch.

Criminal Ties.name: Criminal Ties
Criminal Ties.description:
🕵️ Someone close to you lives outside the law: a broker, a fence, a smuggler or an old gang family.

🗣️ You know how that world talks and how to keep a straight face.
⚠️ You hold numbers you should not have.

📈 Grants: Speed +1, Streetwise +5, Deception +5
🎒 Starts with: Burner phone
Criminal Ties.traitNarrativeEffects: Someone close (kin or family friend) works in crime: broker, fence, smuggler, loan shark, gambler, or an old yakuza family, now a designated villain group under police watch. Never canon. The player may define who and how close; else the narrator picks one contact, kept human: loyal their way, dangerous, often in trouble. The character is no criminal unless the player says so. In play: burner-phone numbers reach a broker, a no-questions doctor or a place to lie low; every favor is a debt due at a bad moment. Old associates may ask for a job, a lookout or silence. Pressure: police may know the family name; agencies and the Hero Public Safety Commission check backgrounds, and exposed ties bring hard questions. Heroes may want an informant; villains, a recruit or risk. Paths: a hero student's secret may surface at the worst time; a villain finds doors open, debts owed. Childhood: silence to police, leaving for business talk, knowing whose streets were whose.

Grew Up Facing Prejudice.name: Grew Up Facing Prejudice
Grew Up Facing Prejudice.description:
🛡️ You grew up with stares, insults and closed doors: as a heteromorph, as someone born Quirkless or with a Quirk people call villainous.

🧱 You learned to hold your ground.
👁️ You can tell kindness from pity.

📈 Grants: Endurance +1, Willpower +5, Insight +5
Grew Up Facing Prejudice.traitNarrativeEffects: It depends on the character. Heteromorph (Mutant Type): stares, people crossing the street, refused service, landlords and other parents calling them dangerous, open hostility in some rural towns. Quirkless: pity, bullying, teachers and doctors urging them to give up heroics, a class joke from age four. Neither: a Quirk people called villainous or frightening. In play: most people in Musutafu and at U.A. are polite; some are not. The narrator shows it in small fitting moments (a double take, a clerk's hesitation, a reporter's angle, a hero assuming the worst) and shows people who do better. Willpower and Insight help read and withstand it, not end it. Pressure: villain and extremist recruiters seek this history, offering belonging and a target for anger; allies, mentors and others like them offer another way; the narrator surfaces both, the player decides. Childhood: safe places, a neutral face, whispers, the few who treated them as ordinary.

Family Business.name: Family Business
Family Business.description:
🏮 Your family runs a small business: a shop, a restaurant or a workshop.

🧾 You grew up behind the counter, serving customers and bargaining with suppliers.
🛠️ You learned the work with your hands.

📈 Grants: Technique +1, Hospitality +5, Negotiation +5
Family Business.traitNarrativeEffects: Family runs a small business; player picks the kind (shop, restaurant or workshop) and place, default a small restaurant in an older Musutafu shopping arcade. Both are original characters. In play: a place to return to, work a shift, hear local news, bring classmates; regulars are ordinary people, sometimes a local pro or police officer. Risks: rent, chain stores, slow seasons, villain fights wrecking the street, who pays hero property damage, thugs selling protection. Pressure: help expected when short-staffed; the family may hope they take over. Shifts earn meals and goodwill, not wages; money is tight. A business crisis is a story opportunity the narrator may raise, with time to act. Paths: a hero who saves the street earns loyal neighbors; a villain or vigilante brings risk to the family's door. Childhood: after-school and weekend shifts, difficult customers, supplier bargaining, late closing; hands trained by knife work, repairs, wrapping, stocking.

Hot-Blooded.name: Hot-Blooded
Hot-Blooded.description:
🔥 You run hot: loud, passionate and first into any fight or cause.

💪 Your energy lifts the people around you, and teammates push harder beside you.
😤 You come on strong: people feel your anger at injustice before you say a word.
⚠️ Easy to provoke: taunts and insults to friends land hard, and hiding your anger is a hard Willpower check.
⚠️ Waiting quietly on a stakeout or staying polite in a tense negotiation takes visible effort.
🔀 If you are also Calm Under Fire, the heat shows in daily life and drops away in real danger.

📈 Grants: Power +1, Intimidation +5, Leadership +5
Hot-Blooded.traitNarrativeEffects: The character feels everything at full volume: shouted encouragement, a fist on the table, a charge toward trouble, anger at injustice that shows on their face. Teammates feed off that energy and push harder beside them. Weakness: taunts, insults to friends and public humiliation land hard. When someone provokes them on purpose, hiding their anger is a hard Willpower check; on a failure it shows (a raised voice, a sharp reply, a step forward), and what they do next is still the player's choice. Villains, rivals and reporters learn to use this. Waiting quietly on a stakeout or staying polite in a tense negotiation takes visible effort. If the character is also Calm Under Fire, the heat shows in daily life and arguments and drops away in real danger.

Analytical.name: Analytical
Analytical.description:
📊 You take problems apart: you notice patterns, keep notes and want to know how a thing works before you act.

🔍 You spot patterns, find the mechanism behind a problem and ask the precise question that cracks it.
👁️ You read people's habits and tells, down to how an opponent shifts their weight.
⚠️ You can think too long: with no time and missing information you hesitate, and a chance may pass.
⚠️ You can come across as cold, treating people as problems to solve, and you distrust feelings you cannot explain.

📈 Grants: Intelligence +1, Investigation +5, Insight +5
Analytical.traitNarrativeEffects: The character watches, compares and breaks things down: how an opponent shifts their weight, why a plan failed, where a Quirk's limits must be. They think aloud, take notes and ask precise questions, and in a crisis they look for the mechanism behind the obvious move. Weakness: they can think too long. When a decision must be made at once with missing information, they hesitate, and the narrator may let a chance pass while they are still working it out. They can come across as cold, treating people as problems to solve, and they distrust a feeling they cannot explain. The narrator may show the urge to keep analyzing; when to stop and act is the player's call.

Calm Under Fire.name: Calm Under Fire
Calm Under Fire.description:
🧊 When things go wrong, you get quieter and clearer.

🌱 In danger you slow down: a level voice, short sentences and eyes on what matters.
🧠 Panic and threats have a hard time taking your focus.
⚠️ The fear waits until the crisis is over, then returns: a sleepless night, shaking hands, a short temper or numbness.
⚠️ Others can read your calm as coldness, especially at a hospital bed or a funeral.
🔀 If you are also Hot-Blooded, you flare up over small things in daily life and go quiet in real danger.

📈 Grants: Willpower +5
Calm Under Fire.traitNarrativeEffects: In danger the character slows down: a level voice, short sentences, eyes on what matters. Panicking civilians and nervous teammates settle around them, and threats get less grip on them. Weakness: the calm has a cost. They push fear and grief down during the crisis and it returns afterward, once everyone is safe: a sleepless night, shaking hands, a short temper or numbness. Others can read the calm as coldness, especially at a hospital bed or a funeral. If the character is also Hot-Blooded, they flare up over small things in daily life and go quiet in real danger. The narrator shows the aftershock; how the character handles it, and who gets to see it, is up to the player.

Earnest.name: Earnest
Earnest.description:
🙇 You mean what you say: you work hard, keep promises and take your duties seriously.

🤝 People trust you to lead, and you step up when a group needs organizing.
⚠️ Jokes, sarcasm and white lies get past you, so you are easy to tease and sometimes easy to fool.
⚠️ You can be rigid about rules, and failures and broken promises hit you hard.

📈 Grants: Leadership +5
Earnest.traitNarrativeEffects: The character is sincere and diligent: early to class, prepared, quick to apologize properly, and true to every promise. Classmates and coworkers hand them responsibility, and they step up when a group needs organizing. Weakness: they take jokes, sarcasm and white lies at face value, which makes them easy to tease and sometimes easy to fool. They can be rigid about rules, lecture others and take failure personally, replaying it long after everyone else has moved on. A broken promise, theirs or someone else's, hits them hard. The narrator remembers every promise they make; which promises to make, and whether to keep them, stays the player's choice.

Quick on the Draw.name: Quick on the Draw
Quick on the Draw.description:
⏱️ You react first: to a threat, a question or an opening, sometimes before you know what you are reacting to.

🌱 In a sudden fight or emergency you act at the first opening, and you are first to move when a blow comes.
⚠️ You jump at false alarms, commit before seeing a feint and sometimes act on the wrong target.
⚠️ Opponents who notice can bait an early move, and waiting for a signal takes effort.

📈 Grants: Speed +1, Dodging +5
Quick on the Draw.traitNarrativeEffects: The character reacts fast: first to move when a blow comes, first to answer, first to catch a falling object or reach for a phone. In a sudden fight or emergency the narrator lets them act at the first opening. Weakness: speed comes before full information. They jump at false alarms, answer before the question ends, commit to a move before seeing the feint and sometimes act on the wrong target. Opponents who notice can bait an early move. Waiting for a signal takes effort, and others may find them impatient or rude. The narrator may show the itch to move first; the player decides whether the character commits or holds.

Meticulous.name: Meticulous
Meticulous.description:
📏 You do things carefully and completely: gear checked twice, technique clean, no loose ends.

🌱 Your work holds up: you practice a movement until it is clean and catch the small errors others miss.
⚠️ Precision takes time you do not always have, and accepting a rough solution under pressure is hard.
⚠️ Mess and other people's carelessness bother you, and you can seem fussy or controlling.
🔀 If you are also Reckless, you prepare with great care, then throw the plan away once things start.

📈 Grants: Technique +1, Perception +5
Meticulous.traitNarrativeEffects: The character works with precision: they check gear twice, keep equipment in order, practice a movement until it is clean and catch small errors others miss. Their work holds up, and teammates rely on them for details. Weakness: precision takes time. Under pressure they struggle to accept a rough solution, and the narrator may show the cost: a door still being checked, a train already gone. Mess, improvisation and other people's carelessness bother them, and they can come across as fussy or controlling. If the character is also Reckless, they prepare with great care and then throw the plan away once things start. The narrator shows what the extra checking costs; the player decides when the work is good enough.

Competitive.name: Competitive
Competitive.description:
🏆 You need to win. You train harder than your rivals, keep score and take the bait of any challenge.

💪 Rivals drive you, and you train past exhaustion to stay ahead.
⚠️ Losing stings and it shows, and you turn shared tasks into contests.
⚠️ A rival's taunt can pull you off a plan, and you may chase a personal win when the team needs support.

📈 Grants: Conditioning +5
Competitive.traitNarrativeEffects: The character measures themselves against others: grades, times, rankings, who lifted more, who made the rescue. Rivals drive them, and they train past exhaustion to stay ahead. Weakness: losing stings, and it shows. They take the bait of any challenge, turn shared tasks into contests and may chase a personal win when the team needs support. A rival's taunt can pull them off a plan. The narrator gives them rivals worth beating and moments where winning and doing the right thing point in different directions. The narrator puts each challenge in front of them; whether they take it is the player's decision.

Kind-Hearted.name: Kind-Hearted
Kind-Hearted.description:
💗 You notice who is hurting and help without being asked.

👀 You spot the person left out, the lost child, the classmate who skipped lunch.
🤝 Strangers trust you quickly, and frightened people calm down near you.
⚠️ Saying no is hard, so you take on too much, and some people take advantage.
⚠️ Hurting anyone, even a villain, weighs on you, and you may hesitate when a fight demands force.

📈 Grants: Cooperativeness +1, Insight +5, Persuasion +5
Kind-Hearted.traitNarrativeEffects: The character notices the person left out, the lost child, the classmate who skipped lunch. They help without being asked and remember small things about people. Strangers trust them, and frightened people calm down near them. Weakness: saying no is hard for them, so they take on too much, and people who notice will use it. A sad story, true or false, moves them. Hurting someone, even a villain, weighs on them afterward, and they may hesitate at the moment a fight demands force. The narrator shows the pull to help and the weight of hurting someone; when the character says no, or strikes anyway, is the player's choice.

Stubborn.name: Stubborn
Stubborn.description:
🪨 You do not move once you decide: not for pain, not for pressure, and sometimes not for good advice.

💪 You stay standing after a hit and keep working after others quit.
🧱 Pressure and pain do not change your mind once it is made up.
⚠️ You rarely change course, even when you are wrong, and you need to see the evidence twice.
⚠️ You clash with teachers and superiors, hold grudges and apologize late.

📈 Grants: Endurance +1, Willpower +5
Stubborn.traitNarrativeEffects: The character holds their ground: they stay standing after a hit, keep working after others quit and refuse to back down once they have decided. That persistence carries them through long fights and long nights. Weakness: they rarely change course, even when they are wrong. They need to hear advice twice and see the evidence twice before they accept either. They clash with teachers and superiors, hold grudges and apologize late. The narrator lets their stubbornness win some fights and cost them some friendships. When they finally give ground, if ever, is the player's decision.

Cheerful.name: Cheerful
Cheerful.description:
😄 You find the bright side and share it.

🌱 Your smile and steady voice keep frightened people calm and help crowds follow directions.
⚠️ The smile hides your own bad days, and the cracks show when you are alone or exhausted.
⚠️ Some people read cheer as not taking things seriously, so your warnings can be brushed off.
🔀 If you are also Cynical, the cheer is real and runs on low expectations.

📈 Grants: Evacuation +5
Cheerful.traitNarrativeEffects: The character is upbeat: they joke, encourage, point out what went right and keep spirits up. In an emergency their friendly voice and steady smile help crowds stay calm and follow directions. Weakness: they hide their own pain behind it, and the narrator may show the cracks when they are alone or exhausted. Some people read cheer as not taking things seriously, so a warning from them can be brushed off, and a joke in a grave moment can land badly. If the character is also Cynical, the cheer is real and runs on low expectations: they smile because they never expected much. The narrator may hint at what the smile covers; the player decides when the character lets it drop and who sees it.

Reserved.name: Reserved
Reserved.description:
🤫 You keep to yourself, speak little and watch a lot.

👁️ You notice what others talk over: a change in a room, a shift in tone, a hand moving toward a pocket.
⚠️ People misread your silence as cold, arrogant or uninterested.
⚠️ Interviews and speeches are hard Media Presence checks for you, and you rarely ask for help.
🔀 If you are also Theatrical, you are quiet offstage and switch on only in costume or in front of a crowd.

📈 Grants: Perception +5
Reserved.traitNarrativeEffects: The character is quiet and private: few words, a neutral face, no need to fill a silence. Because they listen and watch, they catch what others miss: a change in a room, a shift in tone, a hand moving toward a pocket. Weakness: people misread them as cold, arrogant or uninterested. Interviews and speeches are hard Media Presence checks for them, and making the first move in a friendship is harder still. They rarely ask for help or say how they feel, so problems grow before anyone knows. If the character is also Theatrical, they are quiet offstage and switch on only in costume or in front of a crowd. The narrator shows the silence and what it costs; the player decides when the character speaks up or asks for help.

Proud.name: Proud
Proud.description:
🦁 You hold yourself to a high standard and carry yourself that way.

👑 People feel your presence when you enter a room, and some step aside.
⚠️ You hate looking weak: you refuse help, hide injuries and apologize with difficulty.
⚠️ Losing in public cuts deep, and a rival can provoke you by questioning your skill.

📈 Grants: Intimidation +5
Proud.traitNarrativeEffects: The character carries themselves with confidence: straight back, firm voice, high standards for themselves and everyone near them. People notice when they enter a room, and some step aside. Weakness: they hate looking weak. They refuse help, hide injuries, apologize with difficulty and take any doubt about their skill as an insult. Losing in public cuts deep, and a rival can provoke them by questioning their ability. The narrator lets pride carry them through hard moments and lets it isolate them when they need someone. Whether they accept help, admit an injury or rise to a challenge to their skill is the player's choice.

Loyal.name: Loyal
Loyal.description:
🫂 You stand by your people. When a friend or partner is in trouble, you are already moving.

🤝 You cover a partner's blind side, and partners fight better beside you.
⚠️ You follow friends into bad decisions, even when the friend is wrong.
⚠️ Enemies can reach you through the people you care about, and betrayal takes a long time to forgive.

📈 Grants: Team Coordination +5
Loyal.traitNarrativeEffects: The character keeps faith with friends, partners and teams: they cover a partner's blind side, keep secrets, answer when called and defend their people in public. Partners fight better beside them. Weakness: they follow friends into bad decisions and struggle to see their friends' faults. A friend's request can override their own judgment, and enemies can reach them through the people they care about. Betrayal hits hard and takes a long time to forgive. The narrator shows a friend's pull on them; where their loyalty ends, and whether they forgive, is the player's decision.

Curious.name: Curious
Curious.description:
❓ You need to know how things work and what is behind the next door, including the doors marked off-limits.

🔍 You follow leads others ignore and remember strange details.
⚠️ You cannot leave a mystery alone: you poke into dangerous things and lose track of time and safety.
🚪 The story puts locked doors in front of you; whether you open them is your choice.

📈 Grants: Investigation +5
Curious.traitNarrativeEffects: The character asks questions, reads whatever is lying around, takes things apart and goes to see for themselves. They follow leads others ignore and remember strange details. Weakness: they cannot leave a mystery alone. They poke into dangerous things, open doors marked off-limits, ask questions people do not want asked and lose track of time and safety. The narrator surfaces odd details and unexplained events for them and lets curiosity lead them into trouble as well as answers. The narrator puts the locked door in front of them; the player decides whether the character opens it.

Cynical.name: Cynical
Cynical.description:
🙄 You expect people to look out for themselves, and you are usually right.

🕵️ Lies and hidden motives rarely get past you, and you are hard to flatter or manipulate.
⚠️ You distrust sincere people too, and you sometimes miss the ones who mean well.
⚠️ Pushing away real help and assuming the worst of allies can cost you friends and chances.
🔀 If you are also Cheerful, your cheer is genuine and built on expecting little.

📈 Grants: Insight +5
Cynical.traitNarrativeEffects: The character assumes self-interest: heroes chasing rankings, companies chasing profit, friendly strangers who want something. They spot hidden motives and lies quickly and are hard to flatter or manipulate. Weakness: they distrust sincere people too. They push away real help, mock ideals, assume the worst of allies and can miss the person who means well, and that costs them friendships and opportunities. The narrator offers people who prove them wrong as well as people who prove them right. If the character is also Cheerful, the cheer is genuine and built on expecting little from anyone. The narrator shows the doubt; whom the character finally trusts is the player's decision.

Theatrical.name: Theatrical
Theatrical.description:
🎭 You have a flair for drama: big entrances, named moves and lines delivered for the crowd.

📸 Cameras love you: reporters and fans notice you, and a frightened crowd watches you and follows.
🎤 You turn a rescue into a show the crowd remembers.
⚠️ Stealth does not love you: showmanship draws fire, and a speech can give away a plan.
⚠️ A performance that fails in public becomes a clip people share for weeks.
🔀 If you are also Reserved, the drama appears only in costume or in front of an audience.

📈 Grants: Media Presence +5, Performance +5
Theatrical.traitNarrativeEffects: The character performs: they announce themselves, call their moves, pose for cameras and turn a rescue into a show the crowd remembers. Reporters and fans notice them, and a frightened crowd watches them and follows. Weakness: showmanship costs time and attention. They draw fire, give away plans with a speech and struggle to stay quiet on stealth work. Teachers and older pros may see vanity, and a performance that fails in public becomes a clip people share for weeks. If the character is also Reserved, the drama appears only in costume or in front of an audience. The narrator offers the audience and the camera; the player decides whether the character plays to them.

Honest.name: Honest
Honest.description:
💬 You tell the truth, even when it costs you.

🤝 People believe you, and your word carries weight with teachers, officers and strangers.
⚠️ You are a terrible liar: lying, bluffing and holding a cover story are hard Deception checks for you.
⚠️ Keeping secrets strains you, and you say hard truths at the wrong time.

📈 Grants: Persuasion +5
Honest.traitNarrativeEffects: The character tells the truth plainly. People believe them, and their word carries weight with teachers, officers and strangers. Weakness: they lie badly. Lying, bluffing and holding a cover story are hard Deception checks for them, and their face often gives them away. Keeping someone else's secret strains them. They say hard things people did not want to hear, sometimes at the wrong time, and tact takes effort. When a situation calls for a lie, the narrator gives honest approaches a fair chance and lets the hard check decide a dishonest one. Whether to lie at all, or to keep a secret, is the player's choice.

Reckless.name: Reckless
Reckless.description:
🪂 You jump first and think on the way down.

🤸 You have fallen often enough to land well and roll out of a hard landing.
🎲 Risky moves sometimes win the moment, with real odds and never a guaranteed success.
⚠️ You get hurt more often, ignore plans and drag teammates into danger, and examiners take note.
🔀 If you are also Meticulous, you plan with care and abandon the plan at the first surprise.

📈 Grants: Acrobatics +5
Reckless.traitNarrativeEffects: The character takes risks others will not: leaping between roofs, charging a stronger enemy, ignoring a stop signal, pushing a technique to the edge of what they can handle. Sometimes it wins the moment, and years of falls taught them to roll out of a landing. Weakness: they get hurt more often, ignore plans and orders and drag teammates into danger. Teachers, supervisors and license examiners take note. The narrator gives risky moves real odds and real injuries, never guaranteed success. If the character is also Meticulous, they plan with care and abandon the plan at the first surprise. The narrator never makes the jump for them: the player decides when the character takes the risk.

Become Number One.name: Become Number One
Become Number One.description:
🥇 You want to be the best: the top-ranked hero, the most feared name in the underworld or the best in your field.

🏆 Nothing below first counts. Students are not ranked, so your road runs through the Sports Festival, internships and the license exam.
🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: tests, rankings and stages where you can be measured and seen.
🤝 Expect rivals who want the same spot, and top pros who show how wide the gap is.
Become Number One.traitNarrativeEffects: The character wants to be first. For a hero: the Hero Billboard Chart JP, ranking licensed pros by incidents resolved, contribution to society and public approval; students are not ranked, so a student's road runs through the Sports Festival, internships and the license exam. For a villain: the name others fear most; for a civilian or support student: the top of their own field. The narrator surfaces chances to be measured and seen: the U.A. Sports Festival broadcast, agency scouts, internship offers, rankings, rival schools such as Shiketsu, public rescues and big cases. It brings rivals who want the same spot and top pros who show how wide the gap is: All Might, the Number One hero when the year begins, and Endeavor, the Number Two. Pressures: numbers against doing right, credit taken by others, burnout, and the canon year's events reshaping the rankings. Progress comes only from what the character accomplishes; the narrator never makes their choices for them.

Save Everyone.name: Save Everyone
Save Everyone.description:
🆘 You want no one left behind: every civilian, every teammate, maybe even the villain.

💪 You know it is impossible, and you mean to try.
🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: rescues, triage and people who need you in time.
⚠️ Not every rescue succeeds, and saving one person can cost another.
Save Everyone.traitNarrativeEffects: The character measures success by who gets out alive. The narrator surfaces rescue opportunities: collapsed buildings, fires, floods, panicking crowds, bystanders hurt in villain attacks, Thirteen's rescue training at the USJ and rescue-focused agencies. It brings in rescue pros, paramedics, firefighters, victims and their families, and now and then a villain who might be worth saving. Pressures: triage, where saving one person costs another; the pull to break their own body for one more rescue; orders to pull back; and people they cannot reach in time. Not every rescue succeeds, and losses are never staged for shock: the character gets real chances and honest outcomes. The narrator never decides whom they try to save.

Prove Them Wrong.name: Prove Them Wrong
Prove Them Wrong.description:
💢 Someone said you could not do it: a teacher, a relative, a rival, a doctor or the whole world.

🎯 You mean to make them watch.
🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: exams, the Sports Festival and fights where proof is possible.
🤝 Name your doubters, or the narrator creates them and brings them back at meaningful moments.
Prove Them Wrong.traitNarrativeEffects: The character carries a verdict someone passed on them: too weak, Quirkless, the wrong background, the wrong Quirk, not hero material. The player may name the doubters; if not, the narrator creates one or two original characters (a former teacher, a relative, a rival, an examiner) and brings them back at meaningful moments. The narrator surfaces public tests where proof is possible: entrance and practical exams, the Sports Festival, licensing exams, competitions and fights against stronger opponents. Pressures: proving it at any cost, doubters who move the goalposts, and the question of whether their opinion should matter at all. Some doubters change their minds; some never will. The narrator never decides whether the character keeps chasing the proof or lets it go.

Earn a Living.name: Earn a Living
Earn a Living.description:
💴 You need money: rent, debts, family to support or a life of your own.

⚖️ Every job, contract and offer gets weighed by what it pays.
🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: part-time jobs, contracts, prize money and offers that cross a line.
💸 Pay comes for work done, and rent day, broken gear and bills arrive on schedule.
Earn a Living.traitNarrativeEffects: The character needs income. The player may set the reason (debt, family, independence); if not, rent and tuition are enough. The narrator surfaces work and the price of things: part-time jobs at about 1,100 yen an hour, agency internships, sidekick contracts, prize money, sponsorship and merchandise deals, odd jobs, and brokers' illegal offers that pay more and cost more. Rent day, broken gear and medical bills arrive on schedule. Money is tracked honestly: pay comes for work done, never as a free windfall, and prices follow the world's yen scale. Pressures: a job that clashes with training or classes, an employer who exploits them, and offers that pay well but cross a line. The narrator never chooses the job for them.

Protect My Family.name: Protect My Family
Protect My Family.description:
🏠 Your family, by blood or by choice, comes first.

🛡️ Everything you do is meant to keep them safe and cared for.
🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: calls, visits, needs and threats to the people you love.
⚠️ Keep your identity and address from villains and the press. Danger to family comes with warning and a chance to act.
Protect My Family.traitNarrativeEffects: The character's family, by blood or by choice, is the center of their decisions. The narrator gives family members names, lives and needs (original characters, never canon) and brings them into the story: calls, visits, an illness, school fees, a sibling in trouble, a parent who disapproves. Pressures: keeping their identity and address away from villains and the press, family living near dangerous places, a duty that clashes with a family need, and a family that wants a different life for them. Danger to the family comes from the story with warning and a chance to act; a family member is never harmed offscreen for shock. The narrator never decides what the character sacrifices for them.

Live Free.name: Live Free
Live Free.description:
🕊️ You want to live by your own rules: no contracts, no rankings, no one telling you how to use your Quirk or your life.

🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: open roads, odd jobs and people who live outside the system.
⚖️ Freedom has legal and personal costs, and so does obedience. The choice stays yours.
🤝 Expect offers of freedom with conditions: vigilantes, drifters and villain recruiters.
Live Free.traitNarrativeEffects: The character wants freedom: from rules, expectations, contracts, family plans, or a law that says when they may use their own Quirk. The narrator surfaces both sides: open roads, travel, odd jobs and people who live outside the system, and the limits they push against (curfews, licensing law, agency contracts, family expectations, debts). It brings in people who offer freedom with conditions: vigilantes, drifters, villain recruiters and groups that preach unrestricted Quirk use. Pressures: freedom has legal and personal costs, and so does obedience; the narrator shows both. Never push the character toward crime or toward compliance; present the choice and let the player make it.

Settle a Score.name: Settle a Score
Settle a Score.description:
🌩️ Someone wronged you or someone you loved, and it is not finished. Justice, revenge or an answer: you will have one.

🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: leads, rumors, sightings and chances to confront or expose.
🤝 Define the target and the wrong, or the narrator creates one. A canon target stays true to canon.
⚖️ The law punishes private revenge, and only your own actions can settle the score, for better or worse.
Settle a Score.traitNarrativeEffects: The character carries a grievance against a person or group: a villain, a hero, a bully, a company, an official. The player may define the target and the wrong; if not, the narrator creates an original target with a believable reason. If the player names a canon character, that character stays true to canon and the score unfolds within the canon year's events. The narrator surfaces leads, rumors, sightings, the target's allies and chances to confront or expose them. Pressures: revenge and justice can point different ways, the law punishes private revenge, bystanders get hurt, and the target has reasons of their own. The score may end in an arrest, an apology, a fight, exposure, forgiveness or something darker. The narrator never chooses the ending and never settles it without the character's own action.

Find Where I Belong.name: Find Where I Belong
Find Where I Belong.description:
🧩 You have never quite fit: at home, at school, in your own skin. You want a place and people to call your own.

🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: clubs, teammates, mentors, dorm life and communities that might fit.
⚠️ Some groups offer belonging at a price, including villains who recruit the lonely.
🤝 Bonds grow from what you actually do, and more than one home is possible.
Find Where I Belong.traitNarrativeEffects: The character wants a place and people where they fit. The narrator surfaces chances to belong: classmates, a club, a dorm floor, a team that relies on them, a mentor, a shop or street that knows their name, a community of people with similar Quirks or histories. For a U.A. student, dorm life in Heights Alliance brings shared meals and late-night talks. Pressures: groups that offer belonging at a price, including villains who recruit the lonely; cliques and rejection; and the fear that fitting in means hiding part of themselves. The narrator offers more than one possible home, lets bonds grow from what the character actually does, and never chooses where they belong.

Be Seen.name: Be Seen
Be Seen.description:
📣 You want to be noticed: your name known, your work recognized, your face remembered. Never ignored again.

🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: the Sports Festival, interviews, debuts and viral clips.
⚠️ Attention brings scrutiny too: critics, online mobs, reporters who twist a story and fans who want something.
💭 Attention is not the same as being seen, and recognition comes only from what you do.
Be Seen.traitNarrativeEffects: The character wants recognition: to be acknowledged for who they are and what they do. The narrator surfaces stages and audiences: the U.A. Sports Festival, which the whole country watches in place of the old Olympics, interviews, hero debuts, viral clips, a mentor who notices quiet effort, a teacher's praise. It also brings scrutiny: critics, online mobs, reporters who twist a story, fans who want something, and villains who crave an audience of their own. Pressures: attention is not the same as being seen, and fame can bury the person it was meant to show. Recognition comes from what the character does in the story, never by default, and the narrator never decides what they do for attention.

Fix the System.name: Fix the System
Fix the System.description:
🏛️ Hero society is broken somewhere: rankings, laws, prejudice or the people at the top. You mean to change it, from inside or out.

🧭 This motivation shapes the chances the story offers: student government, journalism, insiders, legal cases and protests.
⚠️ The system pushes back, small wins cost allies, and extremists offer violent shortcuts.
⚖️ Every side gets a fair hearing, and your methods are always your choice.
Fix the System.traitNarrativeEffects: The character sees a flaw in hero society and wants it changed: rankings that reward publicity, laws that criminalize ordinary Quirk use, prejudice against heteromorphs and the Quirkless, how villains are made and punished, or what the Hero Public Safety Commission keeps hidden. The narrator surfaces ways to push: student government, journalism, hero work with a public voice, insiders at agencies and the Commission, legal cases, protests and leaks. It brings in reformers, cynics, officials who defend the system, and extremists on both sides of the law who offer violent shortcuts. Pressures: the system pushes back, small wins cost allies, and the line between reform and destruction blurs. The narrator presents each side's arguments fairly, without preaching, and never chooses the character's methods.

Studied: First Aid.name: Studied: First Aid
Studied: First Aid.description:
🩹 Before this year you trained in emergency care: a fire department life-saving course, lifeguard certification or first-aid shifts at events.

🌱 Bleeding control, CPR and the AED, splints, burns and the recovery position. You work in order: make it safe, check breathing, call help, treat.
⚠️ Crush injuries, Quirk-caused wounds and many casualties at once still overwhelm you.
⚖️ You are no paramedic, nurse or doctor: no prescription drugs or procedures, and you hand patients over when professionals arrive.
🏫 It shows in gloves kept in your bag, a calm voice and a habit of watching everyone's breathing.

📈 Grants: First Aid +15
Studied: First Aid.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained in field first aid: bleeding control, CPR and the AED, splints, burn care, the recovery position and moving an injured person without making the injury worse. At an accident they work in order: make the scene safe, check breathing, call for help, treat. Prior study, not mastery: crush injuries, Quirk-caused wounds and many casualties at once still overwhelm them. Not a license: they are no paramedic, nurse or doctor, cannot give prescription drugs or perform procedures, and hand patients over when professionals arrive. It shows in gloves kept in a bag, a calm voice and a habit of watching everyone's breathing.

Studied: Parkour.name: Studied: Parkour
Studied: Parkour.description:
🏙️ You spent years free-running: railings, stairwells, walls and rooftops, first with a park club and then across the city.

🌱 Vaults, wall runs, precision jumps and rolls. You see a street as a set of routes and pick a line without slowing down.
⚠️ Wet surfaces, unfamiliar roofs and long drops punish mistakes, and a chase across a whole district exhausts you.
⚖️ Running across rooftops and private property is still trespass, and building staff and police treat it so.
🏫 It shows in how you cross ordinary spaces: hopping rails, testing ledges with a hand, landing without a sound.

📈 Grants: Parkour +15
Studied: Parkour.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained in free-running: vaults, wall runs, precision jumps, hanging grabs and rolls that turn a drop into forward motion. They see a street as a set of routes and pick a line without slowing down. Prior study, not mastery: wet surfaces, unfamiliar roofs and long drops still punish mistakes, and a chase across a whole district exhausts them. Not a license: running across rooftops and private property is still trespass, and building staff and police treat it so. It shows in how they cross ordinary spaces: hopping rails, testing ledges with a hand, landing without a sound.

Studied: Climbing.name: Studied: Climbing
Studied: Climbing.description:
🧗 You trained at a bouldering gym, on outdoor rock or with a mountain club, and you know rope work and belaying.

🌱 Knots, anchors and reading a wall for holds. On a building, cliff or rubble pile you test each hold before trusting it.
⚠️ Smooth glass, blank overhangs, crumbling concrete and climbing while hurt are beyond you, and long climbs drain your stamina.
⚖️ Scaling a building in the city is trespass unless a hero or rescue operation directs it.
🏫 It shows in chalk-dry hands, calloused fingertips and an eye that maps holds on any wall.

📈 Grants: Climbing +15
Studied: Climbing.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained as a climber: bouldering, roped climbing, belaying, knots, anchors and reading a wall for holds. On a building, cliff or rubble pile they test each hold before trusting it and move one limb at a time. Prior study, not mastery: smooth glass, blank overhangs, crumbling concrete and climbing while injured are still beyond them, and a long climb drains their stamina. Not a license: scaling a building in the city is trespass unless a hero or rescue operation directs it. It shows in chalk-dry hands, calloused fingertips and an eye that maps holds on any wall.

Studied: Swimming.name: Studied: Swimming
Studied: Swimming.description:
🏊 You swam competitively, trained as a pool lifeguard or grew up diving off a rocky coast.

🌱 Efficient strokes, breath control, diving, open water and towing a struggling swimmer. You stay calm in cold water or a current.
⚠️ Floodwater full of debris, rip currents, deep dives and a panicking adult still push you to your limit.
⚖️ A pool certificate makes you no rescue diver or coast guard officer, and at a disaster you work under whoever commands the scene.
🏫 It shows in a swimmer's shoulders, slow breathing and a habit of locating the way out of any water.

📈 Grants: Swimming +15
Studied: Swimming.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained in the water: efficient strokes, breath control, diving, open-water swimming and towing a struggling swimmer to safety. They stay calm when the water turns cold or a current pulls. Prior study, not mastery: floodwater full of debris, rip currents, deep dives and rescuing a panicking adult still push them to their limit. Not a license: a pool certificate makes them no rescue diver or coast guard officer, and at a disaster they work under whoever commands the scene. It shows in a swimmer's shoulders, slow breathing and a habit of locating the nearest way out of any water.

Studied: Acrobatics.name: Studied: Acrobatics
Studied: Acrobatics.description:
🤸 You trained in gymnastics, trampoline, dance or a circus school, and you know how to tumble, balance and land.

🌱 Flips, handsprings, balance on narrow surfaces and breakfalls. Knocked off a ledge, you turn and land instead of crashing.
⚠️ Great heights, landing with a passenger and aerial moves in the middle of a fight are still dangerous.
⚖️ It is no professional certification, and stunts on public structures still draw police warnings.
🏫 It shows in your posture, your flexibility and the reflex to tuck and roll.

📈 Grants: Acrobatics +15
Studied: Acrobatics.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained in acrobatics: flips, handsprings, balance on narrow surfaces, twists in midair and breakfalls that spread an impact across the body. Thrown or knocked off a ledge, they turn and land instead of crashing. Prior study, not mastery: falls from a great height, landing with a passenger and aerial work in the middle of a fight are still dangerous. Not a license: it is no professional certification, and stunts on public structures still draw police warnings. It shows in posture, flexibility and the reflex to tuck and roll.

Studied: Stealth.name: Studied: Stealth
Studied: Stealth.description:
🥷 You learned to go unnoticed: wildlife tracking, a stage crew working in the dark, or a childhood spent keeping out of someone's way.

🌱 Soft footfalls, shadows and crowds as cover, steps timed to background noise, and freezing when someone looks your way.
⚠️ Sensing Quirks, trained guards, cameras and alarms still catch you, and long hiding strains your patience and muscles.
⚖️ Slipping into a building or past a police line is trespass or obstruction, whatever the reason.
🏫 It shows in a quiet tread, a habit of standing near exits and clothes that draw no attention.

📈 Grants: Stealth +15
Studied: Stealth.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has practiced moving unseen: soft footfalls, using shadows and crowds as cover, timing steps to background noise and freezing when someone looks their way. Prior study, not mastery: sensing Quirks, trained guards, cameras and alarms still catch them, and hiding for a long time strains their patience and muscles. Not a license: slipping into a building or past a police line is trespass or obstruction whatever the reason. It shows in a quiet tread, a habit of standing near exits and clothes that draw no attention.

Studied: Striking.name: Studied: Striking
Studied: Striking.description:
🥊 You trained in a striking art: boxing, karate, kickboxing or Muay Thai, at a gym, a dojo or on a school team.

🌱 Guard, footwork, punches, kicks, elbows and knees with the hips behind them. You know how to hit without breaking your own hand.
⚠️ A heavy brawler, a heteromorph's armored hide or a Quirk-boosted opponent can still overpower you, and street fights have no referee.
⚖️ Hitting someone outside sport or self-defense is assault, and courts look hard at a trained fighter's claim of self-defense.
🏫 It shows in knuckle calluses, a squared stance when tense and calm on a crowded train.

📈 Grants: Striking +15
Studied: Striking.traitNarrativeEffects: The character has trained to strike: a guard, footwork, punches, kicks, elbows and knees thrown with the hips behind them, and the conditioning of sparring rounds. They know how to hit without breaking their own hand. Prior study, not mastery: a heavy brawler, a heteromorph's armored hide or a Quirk-boosted opponent can still overpower them, and street fights have no referee. Not a license: hitting someone outside sport or self-defense is assault, and courts look hard at a trained fighter's claim of self-defense. It shows in knuckle calluses, a squared stance when tense and calm on a crowded train.

Studied: Grappling.name: Studied: Grappling
Studied: Grappling.description:
🤼 You trained in judo, wrestling, jiu-jitsu or sambo, and you know throws, pins and escapes.
