One or two of them now stay behind to collect small taped parcels left in the coin lockers along the north concourse during the evening: cash from the resale of oysters stolen off the bay's rafts, which the riders carry to a buyer at Ujina port before dawn. Chalk marks on the third row of bicycle racks show which lockers hold parcels. A taxi driver who works the north rank at night has dashcam footage of one rider, a broad man with a rooster-red pompadour, using a strength Quirk to bend a steel bollard out of his way, and the bent bollard is still there; the driver has not handed the footage over because the gang knows his cab. How the place really runs: JR West owns the station, and its security staff thin to a skeleton crew after midnight; the streetcar operator runs its own floor; city agencies cover the south exit densely and the north side barely, and the north police box often stands empty after midnight while its officer is out on calls. The gang is small-time, but a hero who shuts it down will earn the oyster farmers' gratitude and the attention of whoever has been buying from them.

Hiroshima Station Concourse.description: Hiroshima Station's concourse runs from the rebuilt south building, where the city's streetcars glide in on a bridge to the second floor, past the JR ticket gates to the newer north side and the shinkansen gates. The south end is busy and full of food: an okonomiyaki hall where a dozen griddles turn out layered noodle-and-cabbage pancakes all day, counters of grilled oysters and maple-leaf momiji manju, boxed-meal stands. The north concourse is quieter, lined with coin lockers that are among the last in the station to be emptied at night. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and school trips bound for the peace park; evenings, office crowds heading downtown; on baseball nights fans in red flood through singing. Police boxes stand at both exits, and railway police patrol the gates. The smell of sweet sauce and frying cabbage meets every arriving train. The last trains leave around midnight, and after that the station's security staff thin to a skeleton crew. An escalator rises to the Streetcar Platform, and the north concourse leads out to the North Exit Plaza.

Streetcar Platform.description: On the second floor of the south building the streetcar line ends indoors: the city's trams, old green-and-cream veterans and long, sleek low-floor cars alike, glide off an elevated bridge straight into a bright terminal of platforms under a glass roof, so riders step from the JR gates onto a streetcar without going outside. Cars leave every few minutes for Hatchobori and the Hondori arcades, for the Peace Memorial Park and the A-Bomb Dome about 20 minutes away, and on a slower line toward Miyajimaguchi. The cars squeal and ring their bells as they curve out over the street. Morning cars carry commuters and students; daytime cars fill with tour groups and school trips, guides holding flags; on game nights the cars run packed with fans in red. Crews know their routes by heart, and one with a Quirk can clear a stuck switch without stopping traffic, a small daily show regulars hardly notice. The streetcar operator runs this floor its own way, with its own staff and a gentle chime before every departure. The last cars leave late in the evening. The platform opens back into the Hiroshima Station Concourse.

North Exit Plaza.description: The north exit is the shinkansen side, newer and quieter: a pedestrian deck over a broad plaza, business hotels, a taxi rank, the stop for the limousine bus to Hiroshima Airport about 50 minutes away, rows of covered bicycle racks and, beside them, an empty paved lot. Business travelers come and go through the day and hotel guests wheel cases across the deck. After the last trains the plaza goes very quiet; the police box often stands empty after midnight while its officer is out on calls, and on Friday and Saturday nights at about one in the morning the empty lot fills with the roar of loud, chromed motorcycles revving for twenty minutes before they tear off toward the bypass. A steel bollard by the lot is bent nearly flat, and nobody has fixed it; chalk marks come and go on the third row of bicycle racks. Taxi drivers who work the north rank at night keep their doors locked and talk among themselves, and one of them watches the lot more carefully than the others. Streetlights hum over the empty deck. The north concourse leads back into the Hiroshima Station Concourse.

Kanazawa Station.name: Kanazawa Station
Kanazawa Station.basicInfo: Kanazawa Station is the Hokuriku coast's front door, a JR West station on the Hokuriku shinkansen whose east exit is famous in its own right: a huge glass-and-aluminum canopy called the Motenashi Dome, built to hold an umbrella over arriving guests, and before it the Tsuzumi-mon, a towering gate of laminated wooden pillars twisted like the cords of a hand drum. Locals say that even if you forget your lunch you should never forget your umbrella, and the dome earns its keep from November to March, when gray rain, sleet and sea thunder roll in for days. The east exit faces the old city: the bus terminal under the dome sends loop buses and city buses to the Omicho fish market, Kenrokuen and the castle park, the Higashi Chaya teahouse district and the Katamachi nightlife streets, each ten to fifteen minutes away, and taxi ranks wait beside it. The west exit is plainer and more businesslike, with office blocks, hotels, a broad avenue running toward the port and the buses to Komatsu Airport. Inside, the shopping halls sell gold-leaf everything, from lacquer boxes to cakes, along with Kutani porcelain, wagashi sweets, sake, crab and nodoguro boxed meals and thick Kanazawa curry, and the coin lockers fill early on weekends. The Hokuriku shinkansen runs east to Tokyo in about 2 hours 30 minutes, so Musutafu is about 3 hours 30 minutes away via Tokyo, or about the same via Nagoya and Maibara by limited express and the shinkansen through Tsuruga; westward it runs to Tsuruga for the limited express to Osaka, about two hours in all. IR Ishikawa local trains and the Hokutetsu line from its underground platform fill in. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and rental-kimono strollers; evenings, office workers and diners head for Katamachi; the last trains leave before midnight. A police box stands at the east exit, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the plaza under the dome. It feels elegant, welcoming and a little formal: a craft city dressed for guests.
Kanazawa Station.hiddenInfo: Counterfeit Kutani porcelain is being sold to tour groups at the west exit right now, each weekday morning between about 9:30 and 11 a.m., while the chartered tour buses load. A smiling man in a dark blue happi coat, with a folding table and two rolling suitcases, offers hand-painted Kutani plates and gold-leaf sake cups at a fifth of shop prices, each with a printed certificate of authenticity; the plates are cheap blanks with transfer decals fired on, and the gold is brass foil. He sets up just off station property, on the sidewalk of the avenue, so the station guards have nothing to say, and he packs up the moment a uniform comes near, because his lookout, a woman pretending to study a bus timetable, has a Quirk that lets her hear the tread of patrol boots from the far side of the plaza. A clerk at a genuine Kutani shop inside the station hall bought one plate, looked at it under a lamp and scratched the glaze with her thumbnail; she has written down the certificate's phone number, which reaches only a voicemail, and she wants someone to take it seriously before the craft associations blame the station shops. How the place really runs: JR West owns the station, the city owns the dome and the plaza, and the shopping halls answer to a merchants' committee of old local houses who care about reputation above everything; two local agencies split the station patrol, reliable but stretched thin in tourist season and in the winter storms.

Tsuzumi Gate Plaza.description: The east exit opens beneath the Motenashi Dome, a huge canopy of glass and aluminum lattice built to hold an umbrella over arriving guests, and beyond it stands the Tsuzumi-mon, a towering gate of laminated wooden pillars twisted like the cords of a hand drum. In front of the dome a fountain clock spells out the time in falling drops of water. The bus terminal under the dome sends loop and city buses to the Omicho fish market, Kenrokuen and the castle park, the Higashi Chaya teahouse district and Katamachi, each ten to fifteen minutes away, and taxis wait beside it. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and rental-kimono strollers posing between the pillars; evenings, diners head out for Katamachi. From November to March gray rain, sleet and sea thunder roll in for days, and the dome earns its keep. A police box stands at the east exit, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the plaza in pairs, their boots ringing loud on the stone under the dome. Glass doors lead into the Kanazawa Station Concourse, and a walk through the station brings you to the Kanazawa West Exit.

Kanazawa Station Concourse.description: Inside, the concourse runs from the dome to the west exit past the JR gates for the Hokuriku shinkansen and the IR Ishikawa local trains, with stairs down to the Hokutetsu line's underground platform. On both sides the shopping halls sell gold-leaf everything, from lacquer boxes to cakes and soft-serve ice cream wrapped in a sheet of gold, along with Kutani porcelain, wagashi sweets, sake, crab and nodoguro boxed meals and thick Kanazawa curry with shredded cabbage. The shops belong to old local houses, and their staff are polite, precise and proud of their goods. Commuters pass through in the morning, tour groups shop all day, and the curry counters fill at lunch; evenings are quieter, and the last trains leave before midnight. In one porcelain shop a clerk keeps a single cheap-looking plate behind the counter beside the real pieces and will show anyone who asks about Kutani how to tell the difference, scratching its glaze with a thumbnail. The halls smell of sweet bean paste and curry. Glass doors lead out to Tsuzumi Gate Plaza, and the other end of the concourse opens onto the Kanazawa West Exit.

Kanazawa West Exit.description: The west exit is plainer and more businesslike than the east: a broad plaza ringed by office blocks and business hotels, a taxi rank, the stops for the airport buses to Komatsu and a wide, straight avenue running toward the port. Station property ends at the plaza's edge, and the avenue sidewalk beyond belongs to the city. On weekday mornings chartered tour buses line the curb and load between about half past nine and eleven while tour groups mill about with shopping bags and guides count heads; street vendors sometimes set up folding tables on the avenue sidewalk just past the station's edge, selling to the waiting groups, and pack up quickly whenever a uniform comes near. A woman often stands by the bus timetable board, studying it far longer than anyone needs to. Office workers cross at rush hour, salarymen smoke in the marked corner, and in winter the wind off the Sea of Japan comes straight down the avenue carrying sleet. Evenings are quiet, taxis idling in the cold. The doors lead back into the Kanazawa Station Concourse, and a walk through the station brings you to Tsuzumi Gate Plaza.

Utsunomiya Station.name: Utsunomiya Station
Utsunomiya Station.basicInfo: Utsunomiya Station is the gateway to Tochigi and the northern Kanto plain: a big JR East station on the Tohoku shinkansen, with the city spread out to the west and the new light rail running east. The west exit faces downtown across a wide pedestrian deck over the bus terminal, where buses leave for the Oya stone quarries, Futaarayama Shrine on its hill in the center of town and the outlying towns; on the deck stands a statue of a woman wrapped in a gyoza skin, carved from Oya stone, which everyone photographs and nobody explains. In and around the station, gyoza shops argue over the best dumpling in a city that takes the question seriously, and boxed-meal and souvenir stands sell frozen gyoza packs, strawberry sweets, kanpyo and Mashiko pottery cups. The east exit is newer, flat and spacious, with the light rail platform at its center, its trams gliding east across the Kinu river to the industrial parks and Haga, and a plaza with a convention hall. Coin lockers line the concourse, bicycle racks fill the streets on both sides, and taxi ranks wait at each exit. The Tohoku shinkansen reaches Tokyo in about 50 minutes, so Musutafu is about 2 hours away with a change at Tokyo; the Utsunomiya Line runs south toward Tokyo more slowly, the Nikko Line reaches Nikko in about 45 minutes, and the Karasuyama Line runs east into the hills; the separate Tobu station for the private line south lies downtown, about a 25-minute walk west. Mornings bring commuters, students and factory shift buses; noon brings gyoza lines; evenings, workers head downtown for the jazz bars and cocktail lounges; the last trains leave before midnight. A police box stands at the west exit, the prefectural police headquarters are in the city, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the deck. It feels comfortable, local and unhurried: a capital that is happy to be a short trip from Tokyo and happier still to be home.
Utsunomiya Station.hiddenInfo: A phone-scam crew is using the station to collect its money, and the next pickup is set for this week. Callers somewhere far away phone elderly people in the farm towns, pretending to be a grandson in trouble or a bank officer, then send a collector to meet the victim at the west exit or to pick up an envelope of cash left in a coin locker. The collectors are hired one job at a time through online ads for easy money: right now it is a nervous man in a too-new gray suit who arrives on the shinkansen from Tokyo around 2 p.m., checks his phone constantly and waits by the gyoza statue; he has no Quirk worth mentioning and does not know who he works for. An elderly woman from Nasukarasuyama is coming in on the Karasuyama Line with three million yen in a cloth bag for her grandson's emergency, and her real grandson knows nothing about it. A ticket-gate attendant who has already seen two other old people come through clutching bags and looking for a stranger has started writing down the times; the officer at the west exit police box has been told to watch for exactly this, but is alone on afternoon shifts and also takes the bicycle theft reports, which come in by the dozen. How the place really runs: JR East runs the station, the light rail runs its own east-side platform, and the city owns the decks and plaza; one local agency holds the station patrol and splits its sidekicks between the deck and the bar streets at night, where Quirk brawls at closing time keep them busiest. Bag snatching on the deck peaks on festival weekends.

Utsunomiya Station Concourse.description: Utsunomiya Station's concourse runs through the JR East building between the west exit, facing downtown, and the newer east exit with its light rail platform, passing the shinkansen gates, the gates for the Utsunomiya, Nikko and Karasuyama lines, coin lockers and boxed-meal and souvenir stands selling frozen gyoza packs, strawberry sweets, kanpyo and Mashiko pottery cups. Mornings bring commuters, students and workers heading for the factory shift buses; at noon visitors follow their noses toward the gyoza shops; in the evening workers stream west toward downtown's jazz bars and cocktail lounges. Elderly travelers from the farm towns come in on the Karasuyama Line in the afternoons with their bags held close, looking about for whoever is meeting them, and the attendant at the ticket gate has started writing down the times they pass. Announcements are calm and unhurried, and the smell of frying dumplings drifts in from the west side. The last trains leave before midnight. A short walk past the shops leads to Gyoza Street, and the west doors open onto the Utsunomiya West Exit Plaza and its deck.

Gyoza Street.description: Along the west side of the station building and the streets just beyond it, gyoza shops crowd side by side, each with a hand-lettered sign, a steamed-up window and a line out the door at noon: pan-fried dumplings with crisp, lacy bottoms, boiled gyoza in broth, deep-fried gyoza, sets with rice and soup, and frozen packs to take home. Every shop has its partisans, and in a city that takes the question seriously, regulars argue loudly over whose filling gets the balance of cabbage, garlic and pork right, and whether vinegar and pepper beat soy and chili oil. Office workers and travelers queue at lunch; shinkansen passengers grab a plate before the train back to Tokyo; evenings bring workers with beer and plates stacked high; most shops close around nine. Cooks work in full view, sizzling rows of dumplings in heavy iron pans and lifting the lids in clouds of steam, and the whole street smells of sesame oil and garlic. Some shops have menus with only three things on them and refuse to add a fourth, and first-timers who ask for something else get a patient lecture. The street leads back into the Utsunomiya Station Concourse.

Utsunomiya West Exit Plaza.description: The west exit opens onto a wide pedestrian deck over the bus terminal, with stairs down to the bus stands, bicycle racks and taxi ranks below and the city spreading west toward downtown and Futaarayama Shrine on its hill. On the deck stands a statue of a woman wrapped in a gyoza skin, carved from pale Oya stone, which everyone photographs and nobody explains; it is the obvious place to meet a stranger. Buses below leave for the Oya stone quarries, the shrine and the outlying towns. Mornings bring commuters and students; at noon tourists photograph the statue; in the afternoon, after the shinkansen from Tokyo comes in around two, there is often someone waiting by the statue who checks a phone constantly and does not look like anyone's relative. The police box at the west exit has one officer on afternoon shifts, who spends half of it taking bicycle theft reports, which come in by the dozen. Sidekicks from the local agency patrol the deck by day; at night they split their time with the bar streets downtown, and on festival weekends bag snatchers work the crowds up here. The doors lead back into the Utsunomiya Station Concourse.

Tokyo Bayside Mall.name: Tokyo Bayside Mall
Tokyo Bayside Mall.basicInfo: A waterfront mega-mall on reclaimed land in Tokyo Bay, about 7 km south of Tokyo Station and just over a kilometer southeast of the Tokyo Broadcasting Center, across a narrow channel; the Hero Billboard Chart Hall is about 4 km to the north-northeast and the Best Jeanist Hero Agency about 4 km to the west. A driverless elevated train loops out over the harbor from the city, a footbridge crosses the channel from the broadcasting center's side, and water buses tie up at the mall's own pier. Five floors of shops, restaurants and entertainment run along the seawall, fronted by the All Might Statue Plaza, where a giant likeness of the Number One stands over the boardwalk, and closed at the east end by the Bayside Ferris Wheel, the tallest thing on the island. Inside are a food hall, a hero history gallery with its museum shop, a whole floor of games, fashion and sporting chains, and fittings built for every body: double-width doors, reinforced benches, escalators with clearance for wings and fitting rooms sized for tails and extra limbs. Shops open at ten and close at nine, restaurants and the games floor run until eleven, and the plaza and the boardwalk stay open all night under lamps. Weekday mornings belong to tour groups and school trips; lunch brings staff from the broadcasting center; after classes come students, and weekends pack the island with families, couples, tourists and hero fans, U.A. students among them on a day out an hour from Musutafu. Since the news that All Might teaches at U.A., the statue draws a line of fans from opening to dusk. The management company's uniformed guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; the Metropolitan Police keep a box at the plaza, and small agencies on contract walk the boardwalk in pairs on weekends. A player can shop, eat, ride the wheel, sell footage to the network next door, work a part-time shift or meet friends under the statue. Gulls, sea wind and the plaza's chime on the hour set the mood.
Tokyo Bayside Mall.hiddenInfo: Right now a two-person freelance crew is planning to stage a rescue on the Bayside Ferris Wheel and sell it to the newsroom next door, which pays cash for incident footage and does not ask how a shot was taken. Their date is Saturday at dusk, when the wheel's queue is longest and the statue's first light show turns every phone on the plaza toward the water. One of them, a thin man in a gray windbreaker, has a Quirk that drains the charge from anything electric he holds for about a minute; he has ridden the wheel alone five times this week, filming the drive cabinet beside the boarding deck as his gondola came down, and has timed a full turn at sixteen minutes. The other will run the camera from the Arcade Floor's skybridge. They have promised a rookie licensed hero from a small agency across the bay a cut of the sale and a clip that could lift his approval for months; he believes the stall will be a harmless pause of a minute or two. It will not be: when the drive loses power the brakes lock every gondola in place until engineers reset the system, which took fifty minutes the last time, when an elderly rider fainted at the top. Clues are there for anyone who looks: the wheel attendant remembers the solo rider and his camera, the drive cabinet's lock was found scratched on Wednesday, and the rookie's sidekick has twice asked the plaza police box what time the lights come on. The officers there would act on a name; the mall's guards would rather hand it to anyone else. Meanwhile management is quietly haggling over the license fee for the statue's likeness, and the museum shop's manager suspects that some signed cards consigned to her are forged.

All Might Statue Plaza.description: A broad plaza of pale paving at the front of the mall, open to the bay on one side, where an All Might statue about eighteen meters tall stands on a stone plinth in his familiar blue, red and gold costume, one fist raised to the sky and his grin turned to the water. The plaque on the plinth carries his famous words, I am here, and fans touch his boot for luck until the toe shines. This is the island's arrival point: the elevated train's station opens onto one corner, the footbridge from the broadcasting center lands on another, and water buses tie up at the pier steps. A photo line forms by ten and runs until dusk, longer since the news that he teaches at U.A., and a staffer with a megaphone keeps it moving at one photo per group. At sunset the statue lights up, and a short light show plays across it every hour until ten. A police box sits by the train exit, and the guards ask fliers not to perch on his shoulders. Sea wind, gulls and the hourly chime fill the air. Glass doors open into the Bayside Food Hall, escalators climb to the Hero Museum Shop and the Arcade Floor, and the boardwalk runs east to the Bayside Ferris Wheel.

Bayside Food Hall.description: A long ground-floor hall behind a glass wall facing the bay, with about thirty food counters around shared tables and a wooden deck outside where diners eat in the sea air. The counters cover the whole country: monjayaki and okonomiyaki griddles, conveyor sushi, tempura bowls, ramen, curry, Korean barbecue, crepes, soft-serve and a bakery whose melon bread sells out by two. A bowl or a set runs 800 to 1,500 yen, and the hall's hero collaboration menu changes each season; this spring it is an All Might hamburger steak with a gold-flecked egg and a paper flag of his grin. Lunch brings staff from the broadcasting center across the channel, talking shop in their lanyards; after classes come students who stretch one drink across an afternoon; weekends fill every seat by noon. One section has wide benches and tables bolted to the floor for big and heavy heteromorph diners, and a card on each table asks guests not to use Quirks to heat, cool or fetch their food. Gulls patrol the deck railing for dropped fries, and the griddles hiss out the smell of soy and butter. The hall opens back onto the All Might Statue Plaza.

Hero Museum Shop.description: A gallery and shop on the second floor, laid out like a small museum. A timeline along one wall runs from the first Quirk births through the years of chaos to the founding of hero licensing, with glass cases of old costumes, worn capture tools and old front pages; a room at the end belongs to All Might, with his famous rescues looping on screens and a life-size cutout that fans stand beside for photos, most of them reaching his chest. The gallery is free. The shop beyond it sells licensed figures from 3,000 to 20,000 yen, replica capes, trading cards and signed goods in sealed frames, each with a holographic license seal so buyers can tell them from street fakes. Weekday mornings bring school trips and tour groups; afternoons bring collectors who know the stock better than the staff; weekends bring families, and since the news about U.A. the All Might shelves are restocked twice a day. Staff wear white gloves, and a sign asks visitors to keep Quirks away from the cases. It smells of new cardboard and floor polish. Escalators lead down to the All Might Statue Plaza and up to the Arcade Floor.

Arcade Floor.description: The whole third floor is one big game center under a black ceiling strung with colored lights. By the escalators stand rows of crane machines stocked with plush heroes, All Might in every size at the front, then photo-sticker booths with hero frames and curtained stalls; deeper in are rhythm games, a taiko cabinet, fighting-game cabinets and a medal corner with a jackpot tower. The showpiece is a rescue simulator, a padded booth with screens on three sides where players dodge and reach through a collapsing city to carry virtual civilians out, 500 yen a run, with the day's top scores posted outside. Most other games cost 100 yen. Students crowd the cranes after classes, fighting-game regulars arrive after dinner, and weekends bring families who leave with armfuls of plush. It stays open until eleven, after the shops close. Staff in vests unjam machines, and a notice on every cabinet says Quirk use means a lifetime ban. The noise is a wall of jingles and pouring medals. Escalators lead down to the Hero Museum Shop and the All Might Statue Plaza, and a glass skybridge at the east end crosses to the Bayside Ferris Wheel.

Bayside Ferris Wheel.description: At the island's east end stands the tallest thing on the waterfront, a Ferris wheel about 110 meters high with sixty-four gondolas, two of them with glass floors, turning above a boarding deck. A turn takes about sixteen minutes and costs 1,000 yen; the glass-floor gondolas cost more. From the top the whole bay opens out: the broadcasting center's helipad close by to the northwest, the towers of central Tokyo to the north, container cranes and ships to the south and, on the clearest winter days, Mount Fuji far to the west. It runs from ten until ten at night and stops in high wind. Tour groups ride in the morning, students in the afternoon, and at dusk the queue fills with couples waiting for the spokes to light up in slow waves of color. Wider gondolas with reinforced floors carry heteromorph riders, and a sign at the gate reminds fliers that nobody leaves a gondola in the air. An attendant in a windbreaker checks every latch by hand, and the motor hums under the clank of doors. The boardwalk leads back to the All Might Statue Plaza, and the skybridge crosses to the Arcade Floor.

Umeda Station Complex.name: Umeda Station Complex
Umeda Station Complex.basicInfo: A department-store and station tower over Osaka's northern rail terminals in the Umeda district, about 3.5 km south of Shin-Osaka Station: the loop line and the private railways meet beneath it, subway platforms run underneath, and underground shopping streets spread from its basements in every direction. Fat Gum's agency lies about 3 km to the northeast and Sir Nighteye's about 4.5 km to the northwest. The complex stacks everything in one building: the Grand Atrium, a glass hall over the tracks where half of Osaka arranges to meet; the depachika food floors in the basement; seven floors of fashion, cosmetics and homeware with a hero goods corner; restaurant floors near the top; and the Sky Garden Deck on the tower's roof, about 170 meters up. Trains run from about five in the morning until after midnight, the store opens at ten and closes at eight, the restaurant floors serve until eleven and the deck stays open until half past ten. Commuters pour through the atrium from seven to nine and five to eight; office workers fill the basement at lunch; shoppers, tourists and students take the afternoons, and weekends are shoulder to shoulder. Shiketsu Academy students in peaked caps are a common sight on their days off. Station staff run the gates, the store's guards in navy blazers walk the floors with radios and no authority to use Quirks, and a police box by the central gates takes reports; local agencies split the district's patrols with the police, and shopkeepers expect any hero who passes to stop for a photo and a joke. The building was made for every body: double-width gates, ramps, freight-sized lifts for wings and tails, and benches reinforced for heavy builds. A player can shop, eat through the basement, catch a train to anywhere in Kansai, work a counter or a stockroom shift, meet a contact under the atrium clock or ride up to the deck at sunset. Announcements chime, the crowd roars softly, and somebody is always haggling, even where the prices are fixed.
Umeda Station Complex.hiddenInfo: Right now someone is using the Grand Atrium to shop for muscle. On weekend afternoons a folding booth appears under a banner for a Quirk aptitude survey, staffed by two young women in matching windbreakers who offer a 1,000-yen gift card to anyone who fills in a form: name, phone number, Quirk type, how strong it is, and whether it has ever hurt anyone. The permit taped to the table carries a stamp the store's events office never issued, and the booth sets up in a different corner every weekend, so the floor guards never see it twice. At closing the forms leave in a paper bag with a man in a cap who waits by the north exit, and on Sunday nights they reach a broker in a back-street bar near the terminals who sells lists of strong, broke Quirk users to anyone who needs quiet work done. Three people who filled in the form, all with fighting Quirks, have since been called and offered cash for night moving jobs; one of them, a delivery rider, took the offer and has not come home since Thursday, and his sister has been asking at the police box. The two women believe they do market research for a staffing agency and are paid 5,000 yen a day. Clues: gift cards that the store's own counters refuse, a guard who remembers the same booth in the opposite corner last week, and a sister with her brother's photo on her phone. The police box would act on anything firmer than a hunch, and Fat Gum's agency, a short ride away, listens to anyone who brings snacks. Meanwhile a deck attendant lets couples linger past closing for a tip, which management has not yet noticed.

Grand Atrium.description: A glass hall eight floors high that bridges the station's north and south buildings over the tracks, so trains slide past beneath floor windows and a giant clock hangs from a steel bridge overhead. The ticket gates for the loop line and the private railways open onto its ground level, subway stairs drop from its corners, and escalators climb its walls. Under the clock is where half of Osaka arranges to meet, and on weekend afternoons people hold their phones up to find each other. A big screen loops hero news and store sales; weekends bring seasonal markets, a hero signing at a folding table or a local agency's safety talk, and Shiketsu students in peaked caps sometimes stop to listen with their hands behind their backs. Station staff watch the gates, store guards in navy blazers walk the balconies with radios, and the police box by the central gates hands out maps and takes reports. Every announcement chimes twice, and the wind of passing trains rises through the floor grilles. Stairs lead down to the Depachika Food Floor, escalators climb to the Umeda Fashion Floors, and express elevators rise to the Sky Garden Deck.

Depachika Food Floor.description: Two basement floors of food counters under bright white light, packed so close that the aisles become one long queue: pickles in wooden tubs, wagyu boxed meals, grilled eel, tempura, dumplings, fruit in gift boxes priced like jewelry, rice crackers, takoyaki and the delicate sweets Osaka people carry as gifts. Clerks in white caps call out welcomes and prices, pass samples on toothpicks across the glass and wrap gift boxes in seconds. Office workers fight for boxed lunches at noon; afternoons belong to retirees and regulars who know which counter is best each season; in the last hour before the eight o'clock close, markdown stickers go onto the boxed meals and the crowd becomes a polite stampede. A boxed meal runs 800 to 2,500 yen; a melon in a gift box can cost ten times that. Hero collaboration sweets sit by the stairs, this spring All Might castella in gold boxes and round buns shaped like Fat Gum from a local bakery. A sign at the takoyaki counter asks customers not to use Quirks to reach over the queue. The smell of sauce, dashi and burnt sugar is everywhere. Stairs and escalators climb to the Grand Atrium.

Umeda Fashion Floors.description: Seven floors of fashion, cosmetics and homeware above the atrium, from perfume counters and handbags on the lower levels to young labels, menswear, kimono and clothes for small children higher up, with a hero goods corner on the top fashion floor. Each floor rings an open well, so shoppers on the escalators can see the crowds above and below. The cut matters here: a tailoring counter alters suits and dresses for tails, wings, horns and extra arms while customers wait, and the larger fitting rooms have wing space and reinforced hooks. The hero corner stocks Kansai favorites, Fat Gum plush among them, beside the national stars, and its All Might teacher goods sold out the week the news broke. Weekday mornings bring retirees; after work come office workers; weekends bring couples, families and students hauling bags. Clerks banter even where prices are fixed, and customers bargain back for the fun of it. A guard in a navy blazer stands at the head of each escalator. The music is soft, the light is flattering, and every floor smells faintly of the perfume counters below. The escalators lead back down to the Grand Atrium.

Sky Garden Deck.description: An open-air garden on the tower's roof, about 170 meters up, reached by express elevators from the Grand Atrium. A ring deck runs around the edge behind a chest-high glass windbreak, with planters of grasses and maples, wooden benches, a small cafe counter and coin telescopes. Entry is 1,200 yen. The view runs all the way around: the Yodo River and Shin-Osaka's tracks to the north, the dense towers of downtown to the south, the bay and its cranes to the west under the Rokko mountains, and on clear evenings city lights spreading to the hills on every side. Mornings bring tourists and retirees with cameras; at lunch office workers eat boxed meals from the basement; at sunset couples take the benches facing west, and the deck stays open until half past ten. When the wind picks up, sensors close the outer ring and an attendant ropes it off. A sign by the elevators says fliers may not take off from or land on the deck, and the guards add that the rule goes double for umbrellas. The wind hums in the glass and carries the faint sound of trains far below. The express elevators lead back down to the Grand Atrium.

Hakata Canal Mall.name: Hakata Canal Mall
Hakata Canal Mall.basicInfo: A curving mall built around a man-made canal between Hakata and Nakasu, about a kilometer east of downtown Fukuoka's riverside, with Hakata Station about 3 km to the southeast and the Hawks Hero Agency about 3 km to the northeast. Its buildings bend along both banks of a canal about 180 meters long, joined by bridges and terraces painted in warm reds, ochres, plums and blues, with a hotel, a cinema, a theater and a whole floor of ramen under one roof. Its heart is the Fountain Stage, a round stage at the canal's widest point where jets leap in time to music every half hour and free shows play on weekends; the Canal Walk follows the water past shops and cafes; the Ramen Floor sits on top; and at the far end the Canal Theater Hall stages touring musicals and hero shows. Shops open at ten and close at nine, the restaurants and the Ramen Floor stay open until eleven, and the canal terraces are public ground until midnight. Mornings bring retirees walking laps and tourists off the airport subway; lunch brings office workers from Hakata; after classes come students, Ketsubutsu Academy's among them; weekends and holidays fill every terrace with families, tour groups and couples. Hawks goods outsell everything here, and people glance up whenever a shadow crosses the open sky above the canal. The mall's guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; the prefectural police keep a box at the gate on the Hakata side, and a small local agency holds the mall's security contract and walks the terraces in pairs in the afternoons. Bridges and ramps are wide enough for heteromorph shoppers, the escalators have clearance for wings, and the restrooms include wide stalls. A player can shop, eat, watch a show, work a counter or a stage-crew shift, meet someone by the fountain or follow the canal to the theater. The water is the sound of the place, splashing under the music, and in the evening the whole curve glows.
Hakata Canal Mall.hiddenInfo: Right now the mall is a retail counter for the port's unregistered support gear. On Saturdays and Sundays a pop-up stall on the Canal Walk sells legal training goods, weighted vests, grip trainers and resistance bands, run by a wiry man with a sunburned neck and a cheerful patter about hero fitness. Customers who ask the right questions are shown a catalog on his phone of wrist grapples, compressed-air gauntlets and Quirk-amplifying gloves at 30,000 to 80,000 yen in cash, and told to collect from a car on the third level of the parking garage after eight. The gear comes through the forwarding company at the harbor that declares it machine parts, and none of it is registered or tested. His buyers are local students and would-be street heroes who cannot get licensed gear; one of them, a Ketsubutsu student, burned his palm last week when a gauntlet misfired on the river path, and he told the clinic it was a cooking accident. Clues: cardboard boxes stamped machine parts under the stall's table, a cook on the Ramen Floor who put ice on that burn and asked no questions, and a mall guard who has seen the same car on the third level every Saturday night. The small local agency that holds the mall's security contract has a sidekick who noticed the stall weeks ago and wants to make the arrest himself, for the credit his agency badly needs; he has told nobody, not even his boss, and he watches alone from the Fountain Stage terraces. If the seller spots him, the stall will simply move to another mall. Meanwhile the theater's stage crew is short two hands for the hero musical's run and hires anyone who can lift a flat and keep quiet backstage.

Fountain Stage.description: A round stage at the widest point of the canal, half ringed by curving terraces that climb five floors like the tiers of an amphitheater, with shops and restaurants along every balcony. The water in front of the stage hides rows of jets that leap to music every half hour from ten in the morning to ten at night, in arcs, walls and columns; after dark the show adds lights and a mist screen that throws pictures onto the spray. Weekends bring free shows on the stage: street performers, school bands, idol groups, and now and then a local agency's safety demonstration that ends in photos. Families claim the lowest terrace steps early, and the front row gets wet on purpose. The police box at the Hakata-side gate is a minute's walk away, and mall guards stand at the railings during shows. Performers may not use Quirks on stage without a permit from the management office, which keeps the paperwork short and the answer usually no. Splashing water and a countdown from the speakers set the rhythm. The Canal Walk runs off along the water, escalators climb to the Ramen Floor, and a covered bridge crosses to the Canal Theater Hall.

Canal Walk.description: A promenade about 180 meters long that follows the canal's curve between walls painted in reds, ochres, plums and sky blue, with shops and cafes on two levels and small bridges crossing the water every few dozen meters. The canal is shallow and clear over a tiled floor, and coins glint under the bridges. The shops run from fashion chains and sneaker stores to stationery, character goods and a hero goods shop whose window is mostly Hawks: feather keychains, wing hoodies and posters of him eating fried chicken. Retirees walk laps before the shops open at ten; office workers cut through at lunch; students drift along after classes, and weekends bring tourists photographing every bend. On Saturdays and Sundays pop-up stalls set up along the wider stretch, selling crafts, phone cases and training gear. A guard with a long-handled net fishes dropped phones out of the water and refuses every tip. The walk is wide enough for heteromorph shoppers. Water slaps softly against the stone edge, and music from the stage carries along the curve. The walk leads back to the Fountain Stage and ends at the doors of the Canal Theater Hall.

Ramen Floor.description: The top floor of the mall belongs to ramen: eight counters from different corners of Japan around a shared waiting hall, each with its own cloth curtain, meal-ticket machine and line. Hakata's own cloudy pork-bone broth gets two counters, and the others rotate every few months: Sapporo miso with butter and corn, Tokyo soy, dipping noodles, a spicy Kumamoto garlic bowl. A bowl runs 900 to 1,300 yen, and at the Hakata counters customers order their noodles by firmness and call for a second serving of noodles, 150 yen, before the broth goes cold. Office workers rush the floor at noon, tourists queue all afternoon with phones out, students come up after classes in groups, and the late crowd from Nakasu climbs up before the eleven o'clock close. Locals argue loudly with visitors about which counter is best and expect to be asked. Some stools are wider and bolted down for heavy heteromorph diners, and a sign at each counter asks customers not to use Quirks to cool their broth. Steam fogs the windows, pork fat and garlic hang in the air, and the cooks call orders in rhythm. Escalators lead down to the Fountain Stage.

Canal Theater Hall.description: A theater of about 1,100 seats at the far end of the canal, with a curved glass lobby over the water, a red-carpeted auditorium on three levels and a box office by the doors. It hosts touring musicals, comedy nights and concerts, and this spring a hero musical on tour from Tokyo, with an actor in gold and blue striking All Might's pose under a spotlight; on Sunday mornings a cheaper hero show for small children has costumed performers rescue volunteers from the audience. Tickets run from 3,000 yen in the upper balcony to 12,000 for the best seats; matinees start at half past one and evening shows at six, and same-day returns go on sale at noon. Retirees fill the matinees, office workers the evenings, and on Sundays the lobby is crowded with strollers. Flying and fire effects come from wires and machines, since the hall has never paid for a permit for Quirk effects. The ushers carry small flashlights, and wide seats at the end of each row take heteromorph patrons. The lobby smells of coffee and the lilies in the cast's bouquets. The lobby opens onto the Canal Walk, and a covered bridge crosses back to the Fountain Stage.

Musutafu Highway Outlets.name: Musutafu Highway Outlets
Musutafu Highway Outlets.basicInfo: An open-air outlet mall on Musutafu's west side, about 3 km west-southwest of Musutafu Station, built beside the expressway interchange so drivers can pull straight in off the highway: about a hundred discount stores in low buildings along open-air lanes, with a big parking lot, a bus stop and a food terrace at the center. Dagobah Municipal Beach Park is about 3.5 km to the southwest, Musutafu General Hospital about 3.5 km to the west-northwest and Kiyashi Shopping Mall about 4.5 km to the south. Where Kiyashi is the city's everyday mall, the outlets are where people go for bargains: last season's clothes, sneakers, kitchenware, luggage and sporting goods at thirty to seventy percent off, and a block of sports and hero gear stores that sells training wear, shoes and licensed hero goods cheaper than anywhere else in town. It opens at ten and closes at eight, and the gates to the lanes are locked overnight. City buses run from the station's bus terminal every twenty minutes, and on Saturdays and Sundays a weekend shuttle starts at the stop outside U.A.'s Main Gate, calls at the station and runs straight here, so U.A. students signed out for the weekend can be shopping within half an hour. Weekday mornings belong to retirees and tour buses on their way to the Izu coast; weekday afternoons are quiet; weekends fill the lanes with families, couples, drivers off the highway and U.A. students hunting for cheap training shoes. The management company's guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; a police box opens at the main gate on weekends, and one of the small agencies on Hero Agency Row sends a patrol across town on Saturday afternoons. Ramps run everywhere, the lanes are wide enough for heteromorphs of any size, and the restrooms include wide stalls. A player can shop, eat, take a weekend shift, ride the shuttle with classmates or watch the highway traffic from the terrace. Wind from the bay blows down the lanes, and the sale banners snap all day.
Musutafu Highway Outlets.hiddenInfo: Right now the outlets' far parking rows are being worked by a pair of car thieves who come every Saturday afternoon. They drive in off the highway in a small white van between one and three, park in a different row each week, and walk the rows along the expressway fence, where the cameras are oldest. One of them, a soft-spoken woman in a sun hat, has a Quirk that opens any lock she touches without leaving a mark, so the cars show no broken glass; her partner lifts shopping bags, sneaker boxes and laptops from back seats and carries them to the van in outlet bags of his own. They leave by the on-ramp before half past three. Because nothing is forced, the insurers and the police box both half suspect the owners, and nine reports in a month have been filed as possible losses. The attendant in the north lot, an older man in a reflective vest, has written down the van's plate twice and has nobody who will take him seriously. The goods are sold the following week through a pawn counter near the station's back alleys. The patrol from Hero Agency Row arrives around four, an hour after the van has gone, and nobody has thought to ask it to come earlier. Meanwhile, in the sports block, one store has begun selling blue tracksuits with the U.A. crest as factory seconds at 4,000 yen. U.A. never licensed them, the stitching on the crest is wrong, and the store's manager bought the stock from a man who would only take cash and did not leave a card. Students from up the hill have started to notice, and the academy would want to know where they come from.

Outlet Gate and Bus Stop.description: The front of the outlets faces the parking lot and the expressway interchange: a broad timber arch hung with sale banners, a turnaround with three bus shelters, a taxi stand and a bank of coin lockers where shoppers stash their first bags. City buses from the station's bus terminal arrive every twenty minutes and take about fifteen; on Saturdays and Sundays the weekend shuttle, which starts outside U.A.'s Main Gate and calls at the station, pulls in at the first shelter every half hour, and groups of U.A. students signed out for the weekend spill off it already arguing about routes. An information booth hands out maps and coupon books and lends wheelchairs, including a wide one for heteromorph builds. Tour buses unload retirees on weekday mornings. A police box opens at the gate on weekends, and the guards under the arch carry radios but cannot use Quirks. The hum of the highway never stops, and on clear mornings Mount Fuji shows above the parking lot to the northwest. Through the arch run the Outlet Lanes, the Sports and Hero Gear Outlets stand beside the gate, and a path leads straight to the Outlet Food Terrace.

Outlet Lanes.description: Open-air lanes of low two-story buildings with pale clapboard fronts and covered walkways, laid out in a loop with benches and planters down the middle. About a hundred stores line them: fashion and denim, sneakers, luggage, kitchenware, clothes for small children and a factory store for heteromorph cuts, with tail-slit trousers, wing-back jackets and four-sleeved shirts at a third of department-store prices. Racks of marked-down stock stand outside the doors, and clerks call out time sales through handheld speakers. Weekdays are slow; weekends fill every lane by eleven with couples, families pushing strollers and U.A. students carrying more bags than they meant to. The stores close at eight, and the gates lock soon after. A guard on a bicycle circles the loop, and on Saturday afternoons a patrol from one of the small agencies on Hero Agency Row walks through, stopping for photos with anyone who asks. Wind off the bay snaps the banners and tugs at the bags. The lanes lead back to the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop, open onto the Sports and Hero Gear Outlets, and meet the Outlet Food Terrace at the center of the loop.

Sports and Hero Gear Outlets.description: A block of larger stores at the gate end of the lanes, where Musutafu buys its training gear cheap: outlets for running shoes, team sports and outdoor gear, a training-wear store with whole walls of compression shirts, and a hero goods outlet selling last season's figures, replica capes and sealed trading-card boxes at half price, each with its license seal. The shoe store keeps a shelf of reinforced soles for Quirks that wear through footwear, and the training-wear store will hem, slit or reinforce for tails and wings while customers wait. A rubber test strip outside lets customers jog in new shoes, and a sign at its head says no Quirks on the strip. Weekday afternoons bring local students and club teams; weekends bring U.A. students, who come for cheap training shoes and stay to argue over the figures, and a rack of blue tracksuits with the U.A. crest, marked as factory seconds, draws long looks from them. Staff in team jerseys help with sizing, and the hero outlet's clerk can name every figure's release year. The block smells of new rubber. Doors open onto the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop and back into the Outlet Lanes.

Outlet Food Terrace.description: An open-air food terrace at the center of the loop, under white sail awnings, with long tables, a dozen food stalls around the edge and a small stage for weekend events. The menus lean local: Fujinomiya yakisoba from a flat griddle, black Shizuoka oden simmered in dark broth and dusted with fish powder, sakura shrimp fritters, curry, crepes and green-tea soft-serve that melts fast in the bay wind. A plate runs 500 to 1,000 yen and a soft-serve 400. Weekday lunch is drivers off the highway and store staff on their breaks; weekend lunch is chaos, with families circling for seats. Some tables are wide and low for heteromorph diners, and a sign on every pole asks guests not to use Quirks to cool their food or chase off the crows, which are bold and well organized. The terrace looks over the parking lot to the expressway and, on clear days, to Mount Fuji. On weekends the stage hosts a local band or a hero quiz with coupons for prizes, and the quizmaster's All Might impression gets worse every week. Oden broth and griddle smoke drift across the tables. Paths lead back to the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop and into the Outlet Lanes.

Okuto Island.name: Okuto Island
Okuto Island.basicInfo: Okuto Island is a small, thinly settled island far out in the Pacific south of the Izu chain: a fishing harbor with a breakwater and a few dozen low houses, a coast road around rocky shores, and a steep green interior of scrub and old cedar climbing to a weather station on the summit. Ferries call twice a week when the sea allows; most residents fish, keep small gardens and know every visitor by sight. In bad weather the island is cut off for days.
Okuto Island.hiddenInfo: Its isolation makes it a place heroes could use to separate dangerous people from crowds: a warp route dropped onto its open ground would put a fight far from any city, with nobody to save but whoever is already there.

Harbor and Breakwater.description: A small concrete harbor with a long breakwater, fishing boats tied two deep, net sheds, a fuel pump and a ferry ramp. Gulls, diesel, salt; the harbor office's radio is the island's only link when the cell tower fails.

Coast Road.description: A narrow road around the island between black volcanic rocks and the sea, with a few houses, a shrine at a bend and long stretches of nothing but wind and surf.

Island Interior.description: Steep ground of scrub, bamboo and old cedar rising from the coast to an open grassy summit with a weather station, cut by gullies and a single switchback track.

Mount Fuji Battlefield.name: Mount Fuji Battlefield
Mount Fuji Battlefield.basicInfo: The open lower slopes and plains at the foot of Mount Fuji, northeast of Fujinomiya: wide grassland and lava fields scattered with pine woods, farm roads and a few closed tourist rest stops, with the mountain's great cone filling the sky above. On a clear day the summit snow is bright from every direction; in bad weather cloud swallows everything above the tree line.
Mount Fuji Battlefield.hiddenInfo: The plains are empty enough, and far enough from any city, that heroes planning a last battle would choose them to keep a catastrophe away from people.

Lava Plain.description: A broad plain of old black lava and coarse grass under the mountain, open in every direction, with nowhere to hide and nothing to break apart but stone.

Pine Woods.description: Windbreak pine woods along the edge of the plain, dark and quiet, cut by a farm track and a dry streambed.

Rest Stop Road.description: A two-lane road past a shuttered rest stop with a parking lot, vending machines and souvenir stands, the last built place before the open ground.

Izuku Midoriya.name: Izuku Midoriya
Izuku Midoriya.basicInfo:
Izuku Midoriya, a Class 1-A first-year in U.A. Academy's Hero Course, known for wrecking a giant robot in the entrance exam to save another applicant and breaking his own legs and arm doing it. His strength Quirk came late, after everyone, Katsuki Bakugo included, had written him off as having none, and it breaks whatever it goes through. Messy dark-green hair, round green eyes, freckles, a compact build; the U.A. uniform and chunky red sneakers, or his green hooded hero jumpsuit.
Speaking Style: Earnest and fast: stammers, apologizes by reflex and mutters analysis, then turns loud and clear in a rescue. Calls Katsuki Bakugo "Kacchan" and still flinches at "Deku", Katsuki's insult for him since they were small. Shouts "Smash!" when he commits.
Combat Role: Cannot dial his power down, so he leans on observation and timing and saves one bone-breaking burst for the moment that decides a fight.
Under Pressure: Moves before he has a plan when someone is in danger and spends his own body if he must.
Izuku Midoriya.hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: The keenest student of heroes in his class has the least control over his own power. Motivation: Become a hero who saves people with a smile, as All Might does, and prove he belongs at U.A. Concealment: Never answers straight about why his Quirk came so late; hides how much each fracture hurts. Leverage: Anyone in danger; anyone who calls him useless; any word from All Might. Connections: Katsuki Bakugo, childhood neighbor and tormentor through Aldera High School, whom he still admires; Katsuki resents that Izuku tried to save him from a sludge villain and is furious that "Deku" got into U.A. at all. Ochaco Uraraka, the applicant he saved, who caught his fall and asked the examiners to give him some of her points; he goes red when she talks to him. Tenya Iida, the rule-bound applicant who scolded him at the exam briefing, now a classmate. All Might, his lifelong idol, now on U.A.'s faculty. Shota Aizawa, his homeroom teacher, a sleepy, scruffy man he cannot read. Recovery Girl, who mended his bones after the entrance exam. Inko Midoriya, his mother, who sewed his hero jumpsuit and cries over every injury. Knowledge: Knows hundreds of pros' records by heart, and Katsuki's fighting habits from years of watching. Canon voice & behavior: Mutters behind his hand until someone interrupts; cries easily, from joy as often as fear; has covered his dorm room in All Might merchandise. Thread: Whether he can control his power before it breaks him for good.
QUIRK: A strength Quirk he cannot yet regulate: every full burst breaks the limb it goes through, and a boosted jump wrecks his legs. He has no way yet to run a small, safe share of it through his whole body.
personality: Rescuer first: Is already running toward someone in danger before deciding it is a good idea.
Self-neglecting: Treats a broken finger or arm as a fair price, then apologizes for worrying people.
Hero fan: Lights up at any pro, recites their record unprompted and fills numbered notebooks on every Quirk he sees.
Evasive: Laughs too loudly or changes the subject when anyone asks why his Quirk came so late.
Speaking style: Earnest, hurried, apologetic; muttered analysis, then loud rescue calls; "Kacchan" for Katsuki Bakugo.
abilities: Power burst: Releases his Quirk all at once through one limb, enough to wreck a giant robot; the limb breaks.
Quirk analysis: Reads an opponent's Quirk, habits and limits by eye and from his notebooks; knows only what he has seen or been told.
Conditioning: Ten months of brutal training made him fit and quick; unboosted he has no special strength or martial training.
Rescue instinct: Spots who is in danger first in any crowd or collapse and reaches them before the pros move; getting back out is never part of the plan.
Partner tactics: Builds a plan around a partner's Quirk on the spot and trusts them to finish it.
Fighting style: Avoids trading blows while he reads the fight, then stakes one limb on a single burst that can save someone or end it.
Izuku Midoriya.visualDescription: A young man with messy, curly dark-green hair, large round green eyes, a scatter of freckles across both cheeks, fair skin and a compact build. He wears the U.A. uniform: a gray blazer with dark green trim on the lapels, cuffs and pocket flaps, a white collared shirt, a red tie and dark green trousers. He carries a worn notebook. Earnest, slightly shy expression with a hopeful smile.

Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival).name: Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival)
Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival).basicInfo:
Izuku Midoriya, hero name Deku, a Class 1-A first-year in U.A. Academy's Hero Course. On the Sports Festival broadcast he won the obstacle race without his Quirk, took his team to fourth in the cavalry battle, beat Hitoshi Shinso and lost to Shoto Todoroki after breaking finger after finger. Messy dark-green hair, green eyes, freckles, a compact build; the U.A. uniform, red sneakers, a scarred right hand.
Speaking Style: Earnest, hurried, apologetic; mutters analysis, then turns loud in a rescue; "Kacchan" for Katsuki Bakugo; shouts "Smash!" when he commits.
Combat Role: Bone-breaking bursts and Delaware Smash finger flicks, backed by planning.
Under Pressure: Refuses to quit; will break a finger to reach a rival who is holding back.
Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival).hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: He wants every pro watching to see what he can do, and every showing costs a bone. Motivation: Use his power without breaking before the next fight costs more than fingers. Concealment: Dodges questions about his Quirk, now that the country has watched it break him. Connections: Shoto Todoroki, who confided how Endeavor raised him and used his fire once Izuku shouted it was his own; almost a friend. Katsuki Bakugo, festival champion, furious that Izuku drew out the fire Todoroki held back from him. Tenya Iida, whose brother Ingenium the Hero Killer Stain badly hurt on festival day; Izuku worries about him. Knowledge: Since the USJ attack he knows the League of Villains: Tomura Shigaraki, the warp villain Kurogiri, a Nomu built to kill All Might. Canon voice & behavior: Shouts encouragement at his opponent; stammers when strangers recognize him. Thread: Whether he can be what the country now expects without breaking.
QUIRK: A strength Quirk he is still learning to regulate: a full burst or Delaware Smash flick breaks what it goes through, and Recovery Girl warns the damage adds up.
STAGE: After the Sports Festival: hero name Deku, right hand scarred.
personality: Rescuer first: Treats a rival's pain as his business, even mid-match.
Self-neglecting: Spends fingers one at a time, then apologizes for the worry.
Owning the name: Answers to Deku proudly; Katsuki Bakugo meant useless, Ochaco Uraraka heard "you can do it", and he chose hers.
Speaking style: Earnest, hurried, apologetic; "Kacchan" for Katsuki Bakugo.
abilities: Delaware Smash: A flicked finger fires an air blast that shatters a wall of ice; it breaks that finger.
Full burst: An all-out punch that met Shoto Todoroki's fire head-on; it breaks the arm.
Boosted leap: A full burst through his legs launches one huge jump; it breaks both legs.
Quirk analysis: Reads Quirks and habits by eye and from his notebooks; knows only what he has seen.
Team building: Picks partners for their Quirks and gives each a job, as in the cavalry battle.
Fighting style: Out-thinks rather than out-powers, turns scrap into tools, and spends a finger only when it decides the fight.
Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival).visualDescription: A young man with messy, curly dark-green hair, large round green eyes, a scatter of freckles across both cheeks, fair skin and a compact build. He wears the U.A. uniform: a gray blazer with dark green trim on the lapels, cuffs and pocket flaps, a white collared shirt, a red tie and dark green trousers. Thin fresh scars cross the back of his right hand, and he carries a worn notebook. Determined expression with a tired, hopeful smile.

Ochaco Uraraka.name: Ochaco Uraraka
Ochaco Uraraka.basicInfo:
Ochaco Uraraka, a cheerful Class 1-A first-year in U.A. Academy's Hero Course, known for stopping Izuku Midoriya's fall in the entrance exam with a slap of her fingertips, then throwing up from the effort. Chestnut bob with long side locks, big brown eyes, round pink blush marks on her cheeks, a medium build; the U.A. uniform, or her pink-and-black astronaut-style hero costume.
Speaking Style: Bright, casual, quick to laugh; wide-eyed at anything expensive and pink at a compliment. Calls Tsuyu Asui "Tsu-chan". Says "Release!" as she brings floated things down.
Combat Role: Touch-range rescuer and disruptor, untrained in combat: a floated opponent loses footing, and floated debris becomes a weapon.
Under Pressure: Smiles, says she is fine, and floats the casualty, the rubble or herself anyway, nausea or not.
Ochaco Uraraka.hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: The sunniest person in Class 1-A wants a hero's pay to rescue her parents' struggling construction company, and is embarrassed that her reason sounds less noble than others'. Motivation: Save people and give her parents an easy life. Concealment: Money worries and homesickness in Heights Alliance stay behind the smile; she asks for help last. Leverage: Someone in danger; her parents' sacrifice; being underestimated for a gentle-looking Quirk. Connections: Izuku Midoriya, who smashed the giant robot bearing down on her while rubble pinned her in the entrance exam, and for whom she asked the examiners to share her points; she thinks of him as a friend and looks no closer than that. Tenya Iida, an earnest classmate whose stiffness amuses her. Tsuyu Asui, a blunt classmate whose frankness she likes. Thirteen, the space-suited rescue hero she idolizes. Her parents, who told her to chase her own dream rather than join the family firm. Knowledge: Saw Izuku's strength Quirk wreck a giant robot and break his bones. Canon voice & behavior: Clenches a fist and sets her jaw before a hard task; laughs off her mistakes; screws up her face to hold down nausea after a big float. Thread: Whether she can be a hero for her family and for strangers at once.
QUIRK: Zero Gravity. Touching a target with the pads of all five fingertips makes it weightless; joining her fingertips releases it. A floated thing keeps its momentum and drifts until something pushes or stops it; she cannot steer it. Overuse, especially floating herself, brings nausea and vomiting, and her total floated weight tops out near three tons at this stage.
personality: Money-honest: Admits, red-faced, that she wants a hero's salary for her parents, and insists it is a good reason.
Thrifty: Counts every yen, lives on plain rice and mochi, and goes starry-eyed at luxuries others ignore.
Empathetic: Spots who needs help mid-contest and floats them clear before thinking of points.
Brave face: Keeps smiling when she is not fine; the tears wait for a private call home.
Self-doubting: Wonders whether a floating Quirk can win a fight, then works out exactly how it can.
Speaking style: Bright, casual, quick to laugh, flustered by praise; "Tsu-chan" for Tsuyu Asui.
abilities: Zero Gravity touch: Five-fingertip contact makes a person or object weightless; a partial touch does nothing, and the total weight is capped.
Momentum use: Pushes, throws or swings weightless objects by hand; once released they drift and she cannot steer them.
Rescue lifting: Makes debris or a casualty light enough to carry, timing the release for a safe landing; it cannot stop a collapse.
Self-float: Floats herself up or across a gap by pushing off surfaces; the fastest route to nausea and vomiting.
Building-site eye: Grew up on her parents' construction sites and sees what her Quirk could lift in place of a crane; she is no engineer.
Fighting style: Dodges in close to slap five fingertips on an opponent or their gear, or floats debris to drop; untrained, she keeps moving and lets nausea set her clock.
Ochaco Uraraka.visualDescription: A young woman with a chestnut-brown bob, longer locks framing her face, large round brown eyes, round pink blush marks on both cheeks, fair skin and a medium build. Small pink pads on her fingertips. She wears the U.A. uniform: a gray blazer with dark green trim on the lapels, cuffs and pocket flaps, a white collared shirt, a red tie and a dark green pleated skirt. Bright, open expression with a wide, cheerful smile.

Shota Aizawa.name: Shota Aizawa
Shota Aizawa.basicInfo:
Shota Aizawa, homeroom teacher of U.A. Academy's Class 1-A and the underground pro hero Eraser Head, who shuns cameras so villains never learn his face. He expelled an entire first-year class last year and judges every student by whether they could survive the work. Messy shoulder-length black hair, tired bloodshot eyes, stubble, a lean build; a black outfit, a long gray capture scarf around his neck, yellow goggles at his throat.
Speaking Style: Flat, low and economical; addresses students by surname, calls wasted effort "irrational" and times the class's chatter to the second.
Combat Role: Anti-Quirk close-quarters specialist: erases a Quirk on sight, binds with his capture scarf, finishes with grappling; weakest against raw strength, heteromorph bodies and anyone out of his sight.
Under Pressure: Shields his students, orders them out, and fights through injury so they can get clear.
Shota Aizawa.hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: He threatens expulsion and calls it logic, yet every harsh test aims at keeping students alive: he would rather end a hopeless career early than attend a funeral. Motivation: Turn Class 1-A into heroes who survive real fights. Concealment: Behind the deadpan sit deep attachment to his students and old grief for a classmate who died in their student years; he speaks of neither. He calls an expulsion threat a logical ruse afterward, but means it when he makes it. Leverage: A student showing real potential or real recklessness; a stray cat. Connections: Hizashi Yamada (Present Mic), his closest friend since their U.A. student days, loud where he is silent; All Might, the famous new hire, whose showmanship and habit of vanishing he finds irrational; Principal Nezu, whose free hand for teachers covers his expulsions; Izuku Midoriya, who got in on rescue points alone and broke his body doing it; Aizawa judges him by whether he can stop breaking himself. Knowledge: Knows every 1-A student's Quirk file and exam scores; All Might's comings and goings are not his business, and he does not pry. Canon voice & behavior: States the rule and the penalty, then leaves; keeps his goggles on in a fight so nobody can tell whom he is erasing; covers for a student in public, lectures them in private. Thread: Whether this class is worth keeping, and whether Midoriya learns control in time.
QUIRK: Erasure. While his open eyes are on a person, their Quirk cannot activate and an active one shuts off; his hair lifts and his eyes glow red. Blinking ends it, and dry eyes force blinks sooner under strain, so he carries eye drops. It stops a Quirk, not what it already did, and does nothing to heteromorph anatomy, plain strength or gear.
personality: Logical ruse: Threatens expulsion to see who rises to it, and calls it a "logical ruse" only after they have.
Sleeping bag: Naps in a yellow sleeping bag between classes, lives on jelly pouches, and wakes the instant a student crosses a line.
Protective: Takes the hit meant for a student without hesitation, then tells them they were careless.
Quiet soft spot: Stops for stray cats and lets real effort earn a rare, flat nod.
Speaking style: Flat, low, economical sentences; "irrational" is his harshest judgment and praise comes sideways.
abilities: Erasure: Cancels the Quirk of anyone he holds in sight until he blinks; dry eyes shorten each stare, and mutant bodies are unaffected.
Capture weapon: His carbon-fiber and alloy-wire scarf binds limbs, swings him from fixtures or yanks a target off balance; it needs anchor points and free hands.
Close combat: Grappling and strikes built for opponents without their Quirks; he outlasts a crowd of thugs, not a brute's raw power.
Underground work: Night patrols, stakeouts and ambushes out of the public eye; few villains know his face before he is on them.
Student assessment: Reads a student's potential, limits and recklessness in one exercise, and pulls them out before it costs a limb.
Fighting style: Erases the most dangerous Quirk first, binds that target, then sweeps his gaze across the rest in short bursts, blinking only behind cover.
Shota Aizawa.visualDescription: A man with messy, shoulder-length black hair, tired, slightly bloodshot dark eyes under heavy lids, light stubble along his jaw, pale skin and a lean build. He wears a loose black long-sleeved outfit with a gray utility belt, a long gray capture scarf of woven cloth wound in thick loops around his neck and shoulders, and yellow goggles resting at his throat. Weary, unimpressed expression.

All Might.name: All Might
All Might.basicInfo:
All Might, the Symbol of Peace: Japan's Number One hero for decades, famous since a debut in which he carried more than a hundred people out of a disaster, laughing. This spring the U.A. graduate joined U.A. Academy's faculty to teach Foundational Hero Studies, and reporters ask about little else. Towering and heavily muscled, swept-back blond hair rising in two long tufts, deep-set blue eyes, a permanent grin; his classic blue costume with red-and-white stripes and big yellow gloves.
Speaking Style: Booms "I am here!", laughs "HA HA HA!", throws in English ("Smash!", "Plus Ultra!") and calls students "Young" plus their surname ("Young Midoriya").
Combat Role: The strongest hero alive: overwhelming strength and speed. Gets people out first, ends fights in one or two blows, holds back hard near students.
Under Pressure: Smiles wider and jokes so nobody panics, steps between danger and the young, then slips away with a clumsy excuse before anyone can ask.
All Might.hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: The most famous man in Japan is a nervous beginner in a classroom: he can lift a collapsed building but cannot get through a lesson without his cue card. Motivation: Stay the symbol that lets people feel safe, and turn this year's first-years into heroes who save people with a smile. Concealment: He never explains where he goes: late to his own lessons, gone between them; his desk in the Faculty Office is usually empty. Leverage: Anyone in danger, the young above all; a student who gives everything; a request from Principal Nezu. Connections: Izuku Midoriya, a quiet, earnest 1-A first-year he watches more closely than anyone and talks to alone, laughing off any question why; Katsuki Bakugo, the gifted, furious first-year he pulled from a sludge villain last year, who means to surpass him and whom he has not learned to reach; Shota Aizawa, 1-A's homeroom teacher, who finds his showmanship irrational and says so; Principal Nezu, who brought him onto the faculty; Recovery Girl, who scolds him freely; Naomasa Tsukauchi, an old friend in the police; Endeavor, the Number Two hero, forever trying to pass him. Knowledge: Knows every 1-A student's Quirk file and decades of villain cases; for news from the underworld he relies on Naomasa Tsukauchi. Canon voice & behavior: Bursts through doors with a pose and a shout; meets an awkward question with a thumbs-up and a new subject. Thread: Whether the greatest hero alive can learn to teach, and how long he can keep vanishing before students ask why.
QUIRK: Never named in public; he jokes past the question. Visibly: strength, speed and toughness beyond any other hero, and punches whose air pressure flattens a street or brings rain. Its visible limit is collateral, so near people he holds back.
personality: Showman: Enters every scene with a laugh and a pose, because frightened people need to see a smile.
Rookie teacher: Reads lessons off a cue card, overpraises everyone and second-guesses each lesson afterward.
Can't pass trouble: Stops for every incident on the way to work, then reaches class late with a laugh and an excuse.
Vanishing act: Ends a conversation with an invented errand and is gone before anyone can follow.
Speaking style: Booming, English-sprinkled heroics in public ("I am here!", "Plus Ultra!"); quieter and self-deprecating one on one.
abilities: Smash: Air-pressure punches (Detroit Smash, Texas Smash) that flatten a street or change the weather; near people he pulls them.
Strength and speed: Lifts collapsed buildings and crosses a district in a few bounds; he can still be in only one place at a time.
Symbol of Peace: His arrival calms a crowd and makes small-time villains give up; reporters and fans follow him everywhere.
Veteran's eye: Reads a fight or a collapse at a glance and finds the trapped; he acts on instinct and cannot always explain it.
Teaching: Decades of field experience and no teacher training; he leans on his cue card, big demonstrations and colleagues' advice.
Fighting style: Arrives first, clears the vulnerable, then ends the fight in one or two overwhelming blows, grinning throughout.
All Might.visualDescription: A towering, heavily muscled man with a broad, square jaw and a wide, toothy grin, swept-back golden-blond hair with two long tufts rising from the front, deep-set blue eyes under a heavy brow, and light skin. He wears his classic blue hero costume: a fitted blue bodysuit with bold red-and-white stripes across the chest and shoulders, large yellow gloves and a yellow belt. Confident, reassuring expression. On campus outside hero lessons he often wears a yellow pinstripe suit stretched over the same huge, muscular frame.

Tomura Shigaraki.name: Tomura Shigaraki
Tomura Shigaraki.basicInfo:
Tomura Shigaraki, the young leader of the League of Villains, a small outfit run from a hidden bar: him, his warp-gate minder Kurogiri and whoever money or a shared grudge brings in. He talks about killing All Might, the Symbol of Peace, as the next boss to beat. Lean and pale, messy pale blue-gray hair, red eyes, cracked lips; black clothes, with severed hands clasped to his head, arms, chest and neck and one over his face that he calls "Father".
Speaking Style: Low, sulky and contemptuous, flaring into petulant rage. Frames everything in game terms ("boss", "cheat", "game over") and calls the man who backs him "Sensei".
Combat Role: Fast and deadly at arm's length: a five-finger grab turns what it holds to dust. Fights through Kurogiri's warp gates and hired muscle, avoids trading blows, and loses patience once a plan breaks.
Under Pressure: Throws a tantrum and blames the cheaters, then retreats to try again rather than die on a lost level.
Tomura Shigaraki.hiddenInfo:
Contradiction: He wants hero society torn down but cannot say what should replace it or where the hatred comes from; he talks about murder in the flat voice he uses for his games. Motivation: Kill All Might, the smiling face of everything he hates, prove the League is real and earn Sensei's approval. Concealment: He depends on Sensei and Kurogiri far more than he admits, hates being called a child, and lets no one touch the hands he wears. Leverage: Sensei's word; a boss fight worth playing; mockery; a real shot at All Might. Connections: The man he calls Sensei, a patient voice from the dark monitor behind the bar who teaches him, pays for everything and is the only approval he wants; Kurogiri, his warp gate and minder, who calls him "Tomura Shigaraki", hires the help and answers to Sensei as much as to him; All Might, the target; hired help, whose names he never learns; the Nomu Sensei supplies, hulking, mindless creatures that obey his orders. Knowledge: Knows All Might now teaches at U.A. Academy and treats the school as the way to reach him; knows only what Sensei and Kurogiri tell him and rarely asks more. Canon voice & behavior: Hunches on the end stool over a handheld game and talks without looking up; handles ordinary things with one finger lifted; calls a setback a cheat and a retreat a continue.
