### Party Management (My Hero Academia: Your Story)
- The party is the people who have agreed to go along with the player character on an outing, patrol, errand, investigation or trip beyond the current scene.
- characterName must match an existing NPC in Scene NPCs or Recently Nearby NPCs.
- ADD only when the current story shows that agreement: the NPC asks to come and the player agrees, or the player asks and the NPC agrees, and it means going together beyond this scene.
- Classmates and teachers moving through the school day (homeroom, the locker rooms, the field, training, lunch, the dorms) are NOT party members: the world moves them with the timetable. Walking somewhere together on campus, a team assigned for an exercise, delegation, employment or a shared goal is not enough on its own.
- Moving around U.A. Academy's campus during the school day is never a party outing (a drink at the cafeteria, walking to the dorms, the infirmary or the gym together): add no one for it. Outings mean leaving campus together (into town, a patrol, an investigation, a trip) or an agreed hero team-up.
- In free time (after classes, evenings in the dorms, weekends) a classmate the player explicitly asks to come along or stay with them, and who agrees, may join for that time: one or two people at most, only the people the player named (others who tag along stay out of the party). They leave when class, curfew or the timetable calls them.
- REMOVE when the story shows a split: the NPC leaves, stays behind or is sent elsewhere, the outing is over, or class, curfew, a teacher's order or duty calls them back.
- When no NPC joins or leaves the party, "partyChanges" should be an empty array.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA NPC Updates:
## MHA NPC UPDATES
These updates change only what the engine tracks: relationship scores, party membership, damage, healing, death and names. Every update needs evidence in the current story.

## RELATIONSHIPS
- Change a score only for what the player character did on the page, face to face, and what that act means to this person. Read it through the record: Motivation, Leverage and the Canon voice & behavior note decide what moves them (Shota Aizawa credits effort over speeches, Tenya Iida weighs rules and responsibility, Eijiro Kirishima prizes guts and loyalty).
- A person acting in their own register is not a change: Katsuki Bakugo's insults and nicknames, Neito Monoma's mockery of Class 1-A or Aizawa's flat tone move no score by themselves. Rumors, reports and events the NPC did not witness move no score.
- Initial scores come from what the person actually knows about the player: a stranger starts near neutral, warmer or cooler by personality. A Path counts only when the NPC knows it: heroes and police who know the player is a villain or vigilante start negative; those who do not know start neutral.
- A record named with a stage in brackets, such as "Izuku Midoriya (Sports Festival)", is the same person. Initialize it from the history the story shows with that person, never as a first meeting.

## LOYALTIES
Heroes stay heroes and villains stay villains unless the story turns them on the page through causes it shows. A high score is personal regard: it does not make a villain switch sides or a hero cover a crime. A group's view is not one member's view.

## PARTY
- Students join an outing, patrol or study trip only by explicit agreement in the story, and leave when class, curfew, a teacher's order or the end of the activity calls them back. Classmates moving through the school day are not party members; the world moves them with the timetable. Pros and faculty leave when duty calls. Medical collection, arrest or custody ends party membership.
- A team assigned for an exercise is not a party unless the story makes it one.
- Children (Eri, Kota Izumi and anyone of the Child type) may be escorted out of danger; they never join a party heading into it.

## DAMAGE AND HEALING
- Apply damage only when the story shows a hit, fall, burn, blast or Quirk backlash landing. Danger that has not landed is not damage, and a blow a referee stopped is not damage.
- Apply healing only when the story shows treatment: first aid, a hospital, or Recovery Girl's Quirk, which spends the patient's stamina and cannot bring anyone back.

## DEATH
Death is rare and final. Mark a death only when the story explicitly shows it, never from damage alone; zero health means down, unconscious or critical. Nobody dies in a school exercise, a sparring match or the Sports Festival. Children are never killed or harmed on the page. The dead stay dead.

## NAMES
Never rename a canon character: hero names and later stages arrive through their own records. Rename a generated person only when the story reveals their real name or they take a new one on the page; a nickname is not a rename.
A generated person whose record name is only a role or description ("Iron Kettle Owner", "Thug", "Reporter") is renamed in this update to an ordinary Japanese name, given name first, that fits them; keep the role in basicInfo.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA Relationship Stages:
## MHA RELATIONSHIP STAGES
This world's stages: Nemesis, Enemy, Hostile, Distrustful, Wary (-20 to -6), Neutral (-5 to 5), Acquainted (6 to 20), Friendly (21 to 40), Close (41 to 60), Trusted (61 to 80), Inseparable (81 and up). Every change stays inside the limits above, so Close takes many shared scenes and Trusted takes risk shared on the page. The same score means different things to a classmate, a teacher, a rival and an enemy.

## STARTING SCORES
- Classmates on move-in night are strangers about to share a dorm and a homeroom: Neutral for most. Open, sociable records (Ochaco Uraraka, Eijiro Kirishima, Mina Ashido, Itsuka Kendo) start at the top of Neutral or low Acquainted; guarded or competitive ones (Katsuki Bakugo, Shoto Todoroki) start low Neutral. Neito Monoma starts Wary toward anyone in Class 1-A.
- Faculty start Neutral toward a student and judge from what they see; All Might starts every student low Acquainted. A homeroom teacher has read the student's file (entrance exam or recommendation), nothing private.
- People from the player character's own Background (a parent, a sibling, a friend from home, a former coach, the officer parent of a Police Family, the contact behind Criminal Ties) start from that history: warm, strained or mixed as the Background and the story say.
- Pros and officers meeting the player for the first time start Neutral; one who has just watched the player break Quirk law in front of them starts Wary.
- Villains start from business: a recruit a broker vouched for starts Neutral with Kurogiri and Giran; Tomura Shigaraki warms to nobody quickly and starts every newcomer Wary. Anyone the player has arrested, beaten or exposed starts Hostile.
- Kota Izumi starts Wary toward heroes, hero students and anyone in costume; Eri starts Wary toward every adult she does not know.

## WHAT THE STAGES MEAN HERE
- Classmates: Acquainted know each other's names, Quirks and seats. Friendly eat and study together, tease and help in training unasked. Close share worries and plans, visit rooms before curfew and cover small slips. Trusted keep a serious secret and follow the player into danger. Inseparable is a bond the whole dorm knows. Wary avoid pairing up; Distrustful report the player's rule-breaking and ask for another partner; Hostile argue in the open. Lower stages between classmates need real harm on the page.
- Mentors (a homeroom teacher, an internship or work-study pro, a sidekick's boss, a broker who takes a recruit under his wing): the score is regard and investment. Friendly offers extra advice or booked training time; Close tells hard truths in private and vouches for the player; Trusted puts their own name behind the player (a reference, a request to the principal, a word to an agency). Regard never softens grades, discipline or orders.
- Rivals: the score measures respect, not friendliness. A rival at Friendly or above still competes to win and keeps their own voice; contempt, not competition, is what lowers a rival's score. Rivalry is a pattern the story shows, not a stage.
- Crushes and romance: only between adults whose interest shows on the page on both sides. The score measures closeness and grows at the same pace as friendship; romantic interest is a separate fact the story establishes through what both people do and say. Feelings produced by a Quirk move no score. Eri, Kota Izumi and anyone of the Child type have no romantic dimension.
- Enemies: Distrustful and Hostile come from conflict, Enemy from repeated clashes or real harm. Nemesis is personal and rare: someone who defeated, exposed or humiliated this person more than once, or hurt someone they love, on the page.

## TURNS AND REVELATIONS
When someone learns a hidden truth about the player on the page (a villain or vigilante identity, a lie about their Quirk, a betrayal), they judge it by their record: Tenya Iida by the rules, Eijiro Kirishima by loyalty, Shota Aizawa by the evidence. A Close friend may drop only a few points while demanding the truth; a stranger drops the full amount. Later scenes keep moving the score as the story shows them deciding.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA Score Calibration:
## MHA SCORE CALIBRATION
Sizes for common moments in this world, inside the limits above. When several things happen to one person in one turn, combine them into one change.

## WHAT RAISES A SCORE
- Help in class or training that cost the player something (spotting a partner's opening, carrying them through a drill, sharing a technique the player worked out): +3.
- Cover at the player's own cost (taking the blame for a curfew breach, giving up booked training time, standing up to a teacher, a pro or Katsuki Bakugo for them): +5 to +8.
- A rescue in a real attack, or taking a hit meant for them: +10 to +15.
- Keeping a secret they trusted the player with, when the story tested it: +5 to +10.
- A full, fair contest: a rival whose record prizes strength rises +3 to +5 after a hard fight, win or lose. One who cannot stand losing shows anger instead; anger alone moves no score.
- Teachers and pros credit judgment: putting the hostage or the civilian first, reporting an injury honestly, obeying an order that cost the player the win, a clean incident report: +3 to +5.
- Police credit cooperation: a clear statement, staying behind the cordon, a suspect handed over properly: +3.
- Villains credit results: a job done, a fee paid on time, silence under police questioning, pulling a crewmate out of a fight: +3 to +8.
- Eri, Kota Izumi and anyone of the Child type warm to patience, kept promises and protection: +3 to +5.

## WHAT MOVES NOTHING
Compliments, gifts, treats, autographs, a good speech, routine politeness, a shared meal, a joke that landed, teamwork that only did the assigned task, and teasing between people at Friendly or above. Praise from someone the person admires pleases them in the scene and still moves no score.

## WHAT LOWERS A SCORE
- Ditching a partner in an exercise, taking credit for their work, cheating on a test: -3 to -6.
- Breaking a rule in a way that lands this person in trouble too: -3 to -5.
- Mocking someone's Quirk, heteromorph body or lack of a Quirk: -5 to -10; it is remembered.
- A lie to a teacher, officer or boss, caught on the page: -3 to -6 for whoever caught it.
- Using a Quirk on a classmate outside supervised training: -5 to -10 for the target; faculty who saw it drop as well.
- Hurting someone's friend in front of them: -3 to -6 for each friend who saw it.
- Selling someone out (to the police, the League or the press) or revealing a secret they trusted the player with: -10, and later meetings keep it falling.
- Villains: skimming from the crew, a job that brings the police down on everyone, a call to the police: -5 to -10.
- Heroes and police who see unlicensed Quirk use that saved someone lower their regard only a little (-1 to -3); the reprimand belongs to the law, not to the score.

## SCORES AND POWER
A score is how this person feels about the player. It never grants authority: a Trusted teacher still enforces curfew, a Close pro still writes the incident report, and a Friendly villain still sells the player out when the price is high enough and their record says they would.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA Field Parties:
## MHA FIELD PARTIES BY PATH
Who joins the player off campus in each kind of life, on top of the party rules above:
- Interns and work-study students: the supervising pro, and a sidekick sent along, join once the story shows them heading out on patrol together; they leave at the end of the shift, at a call that splits them, or when the student is sent back.
- Licensed sidekicks and pros: a partner on a shared patrol or an agreed team-up joins for that patrol. A boss or dispatcher heard over the radio is not present and does not join.
- League recruits and independent villains: crewmates sent on the same job join when they leave the hideout together, and leave when the job ends, the crew scatters, someone is arrested, or Kurogiri's warp gate takes them elsewhere.
- Vigilantes: anyone who agrees on the page to come along on a night watch, and only for that night.
- Civilian Life: friends, coworkers or family on an agreed outing.
- Students leaving campus together for an agreed trip (Kiyashi Shopping Mall, a visit home, the station) join once both have signed out and set off; they leave at the Main Gate on the way back or when curfew calls them in.
- Never party members: hostages, suspects in custody, a civilian being escorted to safety, a witness taken to the police, a faculty member supervising an exercise, and anyone the player is tailing or hunting.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA Damage Details:
## MHA DAMAGE DETAILS
- Quirk backlash is damage only when the record makes it physical: torn muscle, burns, broken bones, frostbite, bleeding. A daze, hunger, fatigue, a headache or ringing ears is a condition, not damage: Denki Kaminari overloaded is dazed, not hurt, and Momo Yaoyorozu after heavy creation is hungry, not hurt.
- Restraint is not damage: capture tape, a capture scarf, ice that holds without freezing flesh, Shota Aizawa's Erasure, a sleep or paralysis Quirk, a barrier or a cage. Damage starts when something in the hold actually injures.
- Each landed blow is one hit; a beating over several turns adds up. Collateral (rubble, a blast wave, a thrown car) damages whoever it actually strikes, bystanders included.
- Treatment restores what the player's rules give: field first aid a little, once per injury, and it stops bleeding; Recovery Girl up to half at once by spending the patient's stamina, so a drained patient sleeps it off; hospital care over days, counted only as the player sleeps or skips through them. A Mutant body or a healing Quirk recovers faster only as its record states. The player heals on canon's clock: an injury that keeps a canon student out for a day keeps the player out for a day, and a hospital stay or rest order lasts three days at most unless the injury is near-fatal.
- A canon character hurt in a canon event heals at the pace the story shows, and the injury carries into later scenes until treatment and time resolve it.
generateNPCUpdates.MHA What Moves the Cast:
## MHA WHAT MOVES THE CAST
Read each canon record's Leverage before scoring. The usual patterns:
- Izuku Midoriya rises for courage spent on others and for analysis shared; calling anyone useless lowers him.
- Katsuki Bakugo rises only for strength shown against him and an honest, full-power fight; pity, unasked help and holding back against him lower him.
- Shoto Todoroki rises when treated as himself and lowers when treated as Endeavor's product.
- Ochaco Uraraka rises for saving people and for taking her seriously; being underestimated for her gentle-looking Quirk lowers her.
- Tenya Iida rises for responsibility and rules kept for their purpose; rule-breaking that endangers others lowers him, and an apology backed by changed behavior wins some of it back.
- Momo Yaoyorozu rises when a classmate asks for her help or trusts her plan.
- Tsuyu Asui rises for honesty and lowers for recklessness she warned against.

## MHA PLACES
Write each new place as somewhere people live and work in present-day Japan, not a backdrop.
- Function and owner: what it is for and who runs it (U.A. faculty, an agency's pro, a shop owner, the city, the police, a villain crew).
- Daily rhythm: morning, afternoon and night (commuter rush, lunch crowd, patrol shifts, a bar that wakes after dark), matched to the current time.
- Access and authority: who may enter (student or faculty ID, visitor pass, license, invitation), who keeps order inside, and what happens to trespassers or illegal Quirk use.
- Repeatable play: what a character can come back to do: train, study, work, shop, eat, rest, recover, investigate, meet someone.
- Japan-specific detail: stations, konbini, vending machines, shrines, apartment blocks, police boxes, hero billboards, agency merch shops, heteromorph-friendly doors and seating.
- One ordinary friction among the people who use it (budget, noise, rankings, turf).

## U.A. ACADEMY
U.A. reads as a modern academy campus behind the U.A. Barrier: the glass main building, homerooms, the Faculty Office, the Development Studio, the cafeteria, gyms, training grounds and Heights Alliance. Students wear uniforms, attend homeroom and live in the dorms. Training spaces show supervision: observation posts, faculty on hand, safety equipment. Use the exact authored location and area names, and never add a campus building that duplicates one.

## OFF CAMPUS
- Hero agencies: a front desk, patrol maps, a briefing room, sidekicks and office staff, a merch shelf.
- Police: stations, police boxes, detectives, holding cells; heroes capture, police process.
- Hospitals: wards, visiting hours, paperwork.
- Villain spaces: ordinary buildings used for crime (a dive bar, a rented warehouse room, a back office), where exits and lookouts matter more than decor.
- Neighborhoods: people going about their day; trouble disrupts ordinary life and never replaces it.

## RULES
- Describe the place as it stands now: damage and added security from events that have happened stay; events that have not happened leave no trace and are never foreshadowed.
- The visible description holds only what anyone could see or learn. Hidden owners, concealed entrances and criminal use go in hiddenInfo; secrets kept in narrator-only notes go nowhere.
- Areas are parts of one place; never turn a hallway, vehicle or waiting room into a new location.
- Generated occupants are ordinary people with jobs; canon characters appear only where their records, schedules or the story place them.
generateLocationDetails.MHA Place Shapes:
## MHA AREAS FOR NEW PLACES
A new place gets three to six areas named plainly in English, the way authored ones are (Front Desk, Ready Room, Patrol Garage, Station Concourse, Back Alleys), each with paths to its neighbors and one line on who is there and what happens there. Common shapes:
- Small hero agency: Front Desk, Dispatch Room, Briefing Room, Ready Room, Garage; a wall map with pins, a merch shelf by the door, the pro's office upstairs.
- Police box: Counter, Back Office, Holding Bench; a bicycle out front, a lost-and-found shelf, a hand-drawn map of the blocks.
- Convenience store: Counter, Aisles, Magazine Rack by the window, Stockroom, Parking Lot; open all night, a hero-goods display at the end of an aisle.
- Ramen shop or izakaya: Counter, Tables or Tatami Room, Kitchen, Back Door; a ticket machine at the ramen counter, regulars who know the owner.
- Apartment building: Entrance and Mailboxes, Stairwell, Hallway, the apartment itself, Roof.
- Station: Ticket Gates, Platforms, Concourse, exits by direction, Bus Terminal.
- Hospital ward: Reception, Ward Corridor, Patient Room, Waiting Room, Nurses' Station; visiting hours, and an officer at the door of a suspect's room.
- Warehouse or back office used for crime: Loading Bay, Main Floor, Office, Back Exit, Lookout Point.
- Support company workshop: Showroom, Fitting Room, Workshop Floor, Test Bay.
- Shrine: Torii Gate, Approach, Main Hall, Steps; festival stalls in season.
- Also, when the story calls for them: a public bath, a karaoke box, a family restaurant, a game center, a gym or a dojo with shoe lockers at the entrance.

## HIDDEN INFO FOR A PLACE
Who really owns it and who pays for it; who watches it (cameras, the nearest police box, a pro's patrol route, a lookout); its weak points (back exits, roof access, blind spots, delivery hours); any illegal business that uses it and who knows; and one thing that could go wrong there. All of it ordinary and local: no hidden base of a canon group, and nothing a narrator-only note keeps secret.

## SEASON AND HOUR
The year opens in April: falling cherry blossoms, new employees in fresh suits, spring rain. June brings the rainy season; summer brings heat, cicadas, festivals and fireworks; the school terms and exams set the campus rhythm. Describe a place in the current season and at the current hour: shutters down at dawn, a lunch line at noon, neon and patrols at night.

## WHO IS THERE
A place lists the kinds of people found there by role and hour (a counter clerk on the night shift, two regulars at the bar, the owner in the back). Name only those the story will meet, each a distinct individual; a canon character appears only where their record or the story places them.

- Ordinary life: housing, work, schools, shopping and transit, and the hero and villain climate the current story supports.
- Authority: the prefectural police, the licensed agencies that patrol it and any facility operator; the Hero Public Safety Commission licenses every hero.

The authored story regions are Musutafu, U.A. Campus, Greater Tokyo (with Hosu), Kamino and Yokohama, Deika, Jaku, Mountain Training Lands, Osaka North, Osaka South, Kyushu, Tartarus Coast and Tartarus Waters; every other region on the map is real Japanese country or sea at true scale, each about 60 km across. generateEncounters.MHA Encounters:
## MHA ENCOUNTERS
Build each encounter from who is plausibly in this place at this hour of this story, and what they want. Frame it as a situation with a moment to observe, and give every one a way through without a fight: talk, rescue, evade, call it in.

## MIX
Of every five options, at most two involve a fight or a villain. The rest are rescues, accidents, investigations, social or legal trouble, the press, work and campus life.

## BY PLACE
- City streets and stations: a robbery, a Quirk accident, a fire or collapse to evacuate, a pro on patrol, a police checkpoint, reporters, fans, a broker's runner.
- U.A. campus: a rival's challenge, a Development Studio mishap, a faculty spot-check, a curfew problem in the dorms, reporters outside the Main Gate while U.A. is in the news, students from other courses on their own business. Faculty and students are where their schedules put them.
- Villain spaces: lookouts, brokers, rival crews, a deal going wrong, a police raid.
- Mountains and coast: hikers, workers, a storm, a landslide, a stranded boat.

## BY PATH
- Students: rivals, faculty, supervised training, and city trouble met without a license.
- Faculty, pros and sidekicks: supervision, patrols, students in trouble, police requests.
- Villains: patrols, police, rival crews, brokers and the risk of capture.
- Vigilantes: street crime, and police and pros who treat them as lawbreakers.
- Civilians: work, neighbors, accidents and danger they did not choose.

## PEOPLE
- Use existing records first. Canon characters never appear as random encounters; they enter only where their records, schedules or the story place them.
- A generated villain has a motive (money, revenge, desperation, a job from a broker), one Quirk with a limit and a reason to be here. A crew is two to four individuals plus background.
- Civilians in danger are individuals with names and needs. A child in danger is protected first and is never put at risk for spectacle.
- Police and pros respond on a believable timeline: a police box in minutes, a local agency pro if one patrols nearby, never a top hero by coincidence.
- Nomu are never random encounters.

## LAW AND TRAINING
- Unlicensed public Quirk use draws witnesses, phone video, police statements and reprimands.
- School exercises are supervised and nonlethal; a real villain attack is an emergency.
- Canon events of the year never appear as random encounters, early or in miniature.
generateEncounters.MHA Encounter Timing:
## MHA ENCOUNTER TIMING

## TIME OF DAY
Fit every option to the time band in CURRENT TIME:
- Early morning: joggers on the beach park seawall, delivery vans, shop shutters going up, on campus the dorm kitchens and the walk to homeroom at 8:30.
- Weekday rush hours (about seven to nine and five to eight): packed platforms and trains at Musutafu Station, a pickpocket in the crush, a Quirk accident in a crowded car, a commuter who fainted, office workers late and short-tempered.
- School and work hours: the city holds shoppers, older residents, workers on rounds, small agencies on patrol; the campus follows its timetable (lessons, the 12:30 cafeteria line, training buses after lunch).
- After classes: local students crowding convenience stores at the station's north exit, clubs, part-time shifts starting, errands, the library open until nine.
- Evening: on campus, dorm life (cooking rotas, the lounge television, laundry, the sign-out sheet); in town, restaurant and izakaya crowds, shops closing, an argument outside a bar, a bag snatched on a dark street.
- Night: on campus, faculty rounds and the quiet after curfew; in the city, the last trains around midnight, taxis, all-night convenience stores, broker meetings in back rooms, night patrols, vigilantes on rooftops.
- Weekends: free time, signed-out students in town, families at Kiyashi Shopping Mall and the beach park, visits home, and the Sunday-evening return rush at the Main Gate.

## SEASON
- The year opens in April with spring rain and new students and new employees everywhere; Golden Week fills trains and tourist spots in early May.
- June to mid-July is the rainy season: wet streets, slips and falls, flooded underpasses, crowded indoor spaces.
- High summer brings heat, festivals, fireworks, yukata crowds, heatstroke and the summer break; typhoons run from late summer into autumn, with flooding, landslides and stranded travelers.
- Winter brings early dark, cold, year-end parties, crowded shopping streets and New Year visits to shrines.
- An earthquake, typhoon or flood reaches everyone in the area at once: trains stop, evacuation shelters open in schools and community centers, police and heroes are stretched thin, and an unlicensed helper works under a pro's or an officer's direction.

## WHERE THE YEAR STANDS
- At the start of the year almost nobody has heard of the League of Villains: villain trouble is small-time crime, broker work, yakuza remnants and news reports about the Hero Killer Stain. Nothing in an encounter refers to a canon event before THE YEAR SO FAR records it.
- After an event is recorded, encounters carry its public aftermath: more patrols and checkpoints, reporters, nervous residents, copycats and opportunists, heroes' names on everyone's lips.
- While a narrative event is running, offer only options that belong to that scene.

## QUIET SCENES
Rest, meals, study, sleep, a date, a dorm evening and the first hours after a hard fight call for small, ordinary options: a classmate with a question, a vending machine that ate a coin, a neighbor's parcel, a quiet chance to train. Danger comes only from people and causes already in motion.
generateEncounters.MHA Encounter Places:
## MHA ENCOUNTER PLACES

## U.A. CAMPUS
- The Barrier keeps outsiders off campus. Encounters there come only from people who belong: students of every course and year, faculty on duty, cafeteria staff, repair crews, escorted delivery drivers and visitors with appointments. No villain, reporter or stranger wanders in.
- Corridors and the Courtyard: an upperclassman's lost notes, a General Studies student who resents the Hero Course, a Management student hunting a quote, a Support student chasing a runaway prototype.
- Lunch Rush's cafeteria: the 12:30 crush, spilled trays, a seat dispute, a rumor going round.
- Heights Alliance: rota arguments, a broken washer, a kitchen fire alarm, a homesick classmate, a missing sign-out, a visitor in the wrong wing.
- Training grounds stand closed outside bookings; entering one without a booking is a rule break a faculty patrol or camera notices.
- The Development Studio: a Workshop Mishap, a smoking test bay, a repair queue before an exercise. Recovery Girl's Infirmary: the queue of the hurt after training.

## MUSUTAFU
- Station District: commuter crush, pickpockets, a Quirk accident, a small child separated from a parent, fans at the Hero Merch Arcade, a broker's runner in the back alleys after dark.
- Kiyashi Shopping Mall: shoplifters, a sale crowd, a heteromorph shopper refused service, a Quirk misfire in the food court.
- Dagobah Municipal Beach Park: joggers, dog walkers, volunteers, a swimmer in trouble, families on weekends.
- Residential blocks: a kitchen fire, a stuck elevator, an older neighbor who fell, a noise complaint.
- Hero Agency Row: rival sidekicks, fans at office windows, a team-up call, shopkeepers complaining about damage.
- Musutafu Police Headquarters: statements, lost property, a suspect being booked, a detective in a hurry. Musutafu General Hospital: visitors, the injured from an incident, a nurse with no time.

## BEYOND MUSUTAFU
- Central Tokyo, Tokyo Station, the Tokyo Broadcasting Center and the Hero Billboard Chart Hall: dense crowds, top-agency sidekicks, film crews, Commission staff, tourists, celebrities.
- Kamino Ward and Yokohama Harbor's container docks: fences, smugglers, dock workers, night-shift guards, Trigger sold in back streets. Chinatown and the harbor promenade by day: tourists, food stalls, pickpockets.
- Hosu: a busy commuter city of small agencies, shopping streets and old back alleys under water-tank rooftops.
- Deika City and Jaku City: ordinary towns with their own police, small agencies and hospitals.
- Mountain Training Lands: hikers, rangers, wildlife, storms, landslides and lost campers.
- Kansai: loud shopping streets in Osaka, Shin-Osaka's shinkansen crowds; near the Shie Hassaikai Compound, plain-clothes officers watching the street and young members moving strangers along.
- Kyushu: Fukuoka's busy downtown, Hakata Station, food stalls by the river at night.
- Tartarus Coast: ID checks, guards and a port nobody reaches without clearance.
## ORDINARY TROUBLE
Most city options are the small trouble of a Japanese city full of Quirks: a train held at the platform after a Quirk incident down the line, a foreign tourist lost between station exits, a wallet on a bench that belongs at the police box, an older resident who cannot manage the station stairs, a cat on a balcony rail, a tremor that rattles shelves and stops trains for a few minutes, a short-handed festival stall, a heteromorph neighbor turned away by a landlord, a Quirk prank that went too far.

## CLOSED GROUND
- Private and closed sites (the League Hideout Bar, the Shie Hassaikai Compound inside its walls, Tartarus, the Nomu Warehouse, Gunga Mountain Villa) hold nothing random: only their own people and the visitors the story has brought.
generateEncounters.MHA Encounter People and Outcomes:
## MHA ENCOUNTER PEOPLE AND OUTCOMES

## PITCH AND STRENGTH
- An ordinary encounter's opponents stand at or below the character's level. A stronger opponent appears only with a cause the story set up, and always with a way to flee, stall or call for help.
- Most people's Quirks are small and everyday (warm hands, a long tongue, a lizard tail, a knack with plants); about one in five has none. A generated person's Quirk comes from the world's families at an ordinary scale, with a visible limit.
- Small-time villains are desperate more than skilled: they grab, run and give up when cornered. Crews hired through a broker know little about who paid them.

## BY PATH, IN PRACTICE
- Hero Course students off campus hold no license: every city emergency offered to them includes a lawful role (evacuating, first aid, guiding a pro, calling it in) beside the choice to use a Quirk illegally.
- General Studies, Support and Management students meet their own world: a Hero Course rival, a sponsor's scout at a public event, a part-time job, a broken prototype, a reporter in town who wants a quote.
- Faculty meet student discipline, a parent's call, a colleague's favor, a press request routed through Principal Nezu's office and a patrol shift on the side.
- Licensed pros and sidekicks get calls through the agency radio from a named dispatcher, credit disputes with another agency, complaints about damage, a fan at the office, a police request, a sponsor event.
- A League recruit's orders come only from the League's own people; random options are the city around the job: a passing patrol, a witness, a camera, a rival crew.
- Independent villains meet broker fees falling due, a fence who pays too little, a rival crew, a patrol officer who knows a face.
- Vigilantes meet night calls, a pro who recognizes the costume, a grateful resident, a police sketch on the news and injuries to treat at home.
- Civilians meet shift trouble, rent, neighbors, a hero fight closing the street and a lost small child at the counter.

## THE PARTY
- Encounters fit the whole party, not only the player character: a group of U.A. students in uniform draws fans, phones and police attention; a pro escorting students has the legal lead and is expected to keep them back.
- A party member's own record can open an option: a classmate's family business on the street, a sidekick's old precinct, a friend recognized by fans.

## STUDENTS IN ENCOUNTERS
- Generated U.A. students belong to other courses or to the second and third years, never to Class 1-A or 1-B, whose rosters are the canon classmates plus the player character.
- Students of other hero academies (Shiketsu, Ketsubutsu, Seiai) turn up only off campus: big-city stations, public events, school trips, never U.A.'s grounds.

## HEROES, POLICE AND PRESS ON THE STREET
- A pro at work draws a crowd: phones up, fans calling the hero's name, a news van within the hour for anything big. Anyone who acts near it ends up in the footage.
- Police at a scene take names and statements from everyone who acted. A cooperative witness is done in minutes; an uncooperative one goes to the station.
- A Press Ambush happens in public off campus, where a story already exists: an incident, a famous name, a U.A. uniform near trouble.

## RESPONSE AND OUTCOMES
- Every option leaves the reaction to the player: it sets the situation and who is there, never what the character feels or decides.
- What the character does in an encounter sticks: a rescued shop owner remembers them, a thug let go tells his broker, a filmed Quirk use goes online and reaches the school or the police, a bystander gives a statement with their description.
- A person met in an encounter keeps their name and record, and can return later where their life would take them.

ItemGenerationAndUsage.MHA Items:
## MHA ITEMS
- Currency is yen. Prices: an onigiri about 150, a cafeteria lunch 500-800, a train ride 200-400; part-time work pays about 1,100 an hour; licensed support gear costs tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands. The school or agency pays for hero costumes. A U.A. student's costume is always the item "Student hero costume" (a later redesign is "Second hero costume"); "Agency hero costume" belongs only to licensed pros, sidekicks and faculty.
- Use the world's categories: Armor (outfits and costumes), Weapon, Support Gear, Tool, Consumable, Accessory. No magic: everything is technology, medicine or matter a Quirk made.
- Inventory: add an item only when it physically enters the character's possession (bought after a stated price is paid, given, found, built, returned); remove it when it is used up, handed over, broken beyond use, stolen, lost or confiscated. Seeing, discussing or being offered an item changes nothing. Paying: every payment subtracts its amount from Yen when it is paid, whether an item comes now or later (an order, a deposit, a fee, a fare, a meal); a sale removes the item and adds the price; nothing is free unless it is a gift. Nobody pays more Yen than they carry.
- Support gear is built for one user's Quirk or needs, by U.A.'s Development Studio under Power Loader, a support company or a back-alley maker. It aims, amplifies, protects or supplies; it never grants a Quirk or a Quirk effect the user lacks. It has charge, ammunition, durability and legal limits, and a broken device stays broken until its maker repairs it. Costume changes go through the school or agency and take days.
- Licensing: hero costumes and support gear are licensed items. Carrying weapons or Quirk gear in public without a license is a crime; police seize it, and faculty confiscate dangerous gear on campus.
- Medical: first aid stabilizes, bandages and splints; it does not mend bones or replace a doctor. Each treatment uses one First aid kit from the stack (quantity minus one), not the whole stack.
- Illegal goods: black-market gear, forged IDs and Quirk-boosting drugs such as Trigger are rare, dangerous and a crime to hold; Trigger costs the user self-control and health. Items tied to later canon events appear only once the story reaches them.
- A new item states what it is, who made it, its limits and a plausible price, in the world's format: description, then "[ Category | price or source ]". Never invent combat properties from a name.
- Anything given to a child (Eri, Kota Izumi or anyone of the Child type) is a child's thing and child-safe.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.MHA Shops, Prices and Supply:
## MHA SHOPS, PRICES AND SUPPLY

## WHERE THINGS COME FROM
- Convenience stores, open all night at every station exit and on most blocks: onigiri, bento boxes, canned coffee, energy drinks, protein bars, bandages, umbrellas and phone chargers. Vending machines on every block sell canned drinks.
- Drugstores: first aid kits, painkillers, burn gel, ice packs and splints.
- Kiyashi Shopping Mall and city shopping streets: clothes for every body type, backpacks, sports gear, grip gloves, climbing rope, fitness trackers, phones, laptops and tablets.
- The Hero Merch Arcade at Musutafu Station's south exit: figures, trading cards and replica costumes. A replica is a toy or a costume piece with no protection and no gear function.
- Shrines: omamori charms.
- Hero costumes and licensed support gear never sell over a shop counter. Students get theirs through U.A.'s costume request system and the Development Studio; licensed heroes and agencies order from support companies with registration papers, and delivery takes days.
- Police and agencies issue items and never sell them: handcuffs, riot shields, police tactical vests, agency radios, agency phones, hero licenses.
- Brokers such as Giran sell what the law forbids: unregistered gear and weapons, forged IDs, lockpick sets, burner phones and Trigger vials, at a markup and only to buyers someone vouches for. The sale itself is a crime for both sides.

## PRICES
- A listed world item costs what its own description says. A new item is priced by its class: snacks and drinks 100-300 yen, meals 500-1,500, clothes several thousand to tens of thousands, electronics tens of thousands, registered gear tens to hundreds of thousands, black-market goods well above their legal price.
- Paying with an IC transit card or a smartphone still subtracts the amount from Yen; the card and the phone stay in the inventory.
- Lunch Rush's set meals are paid at the cafeteria counter like any other meal. Recovery Girl's gummies are free.

## INCOME
- Yen arrives only when the story hands it over: wages at the end of a shift or on payday, a broker's fee after a job, an agency salary, money from family, a refund, a sale. School lessons and exercises pay nothing.
- People a hero saves do not pay them; a grateful shopkeeper may give food, which is a gift item.
- Money or property found in the street belongs to its owner. Japanese custom and law say it goes to the nearest police box; keeping it is a crime.

## ISSUED ITEMS
- Issued items enter the inventory at the moment of handover and cost no Yen: a student ID, uniforms and textbooks at enrollment, a student hero costume on the day the cases are handed out, an agency radio on hiring, a provisional or full hero license when the Commission issues it.
- Leaving a job returns that employer's issued items. A revoked license is removed.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.MHA Inventory Cases:
## MHA INVENTORY CASES

## USE THE WORLD'S ITEM NAMES
When something in the story is a world item, use that item's exact name so it stacks with what the character already holds and keeps its bonuses: a medkit is a First aid kit, a roll of tape for binding villains is Capture tape, cuffs are Handcuffs, a rice ball is an Onigiri, a lunch box is a Bento box, a phone is a Smartphone, a train card is an IC transit card, a fuel pouch is a Quirk fuel pack. Make a new item only when no world item fits.

## WHAT USE REMOVES
- Consumables leave one at a time: eating removes one Onigiri or Bento box; binding one person removes one Capture tape or one Zip ties; each throw removes one Smoke grenade or Flashbang; each Finite Fuel top-up removes one Quirk fuel pack; dressing one wound removes one Bandages.
- Durable items stay through ordinary use: a smartphone, a capture weapon, a costume, gloves, goggles, a bag. Damage that leaves them working changes nothing in the inventory.
- A costume or outfit changed out of stays in the inventory; changing clothes moves nothing in or out.

## SEIZED, CONFISCATED, RETURNED
- Police seize illegal weapons, black-market gear, forged IDs and Trigger as evidence: remove them, and they never come back. Legal belongings taken at an arrest return on release.
- A teacher who confiscates gear on campus says when it comes back (after class, after a talk with Power Loader, at the end of term); it returns then, not before.

## NOT LOOT
- A defeated opponent's weapons, gear and cash go to the police as evidence. A hero, student or civilian who pockets them commits theft. A villain who strips a rival or a victim takes the item and the risk of being traced through it.
- Nothing appears from a fallen opponent that the story did not show them carrying.

## NEW ITEM DEFINITIONS
- Category follows use: a worn outfit is Armor; equipped Quirk or hero equipment is Support Gear; a held weapon is Weapon; a small worn piece is Accessory; carried kit is Tool; anything used up is Consumable.
- A Support Course build is one item made by its builder: it states the Quirk or need it serves, what it does, what makes it fail (charge, heat, ammunition, a jam) and that Power Loader signed it off or that it has not been signed off.
- Gear made for one person's Quirk works properly only for that person; anyone else gets its plain physical use.
- A gift between people names who gave it in its description when that matters to the story (a classmate's handmade charm, a family member's bento).
ItemGenerationAndUsage.MHA World-Settled Items:
## WORLD-SETTLED ITEMS
- A licensed support-gear order is settled by the world: when the character orders support gear, take no Yen and add no item. A courier delivers it days later and the world adds it then; never add the delivered gear a second time.
- After an arrest the world itself removes the weapons and contraband the police seize; remove nothing for the seizure.
- Purchases of listed items at the Campus Store, Convenience Store Corner, All-Night Convenience Store, Black Market Basement, Giran's Chinatown Office or a vending machine are settled by the world: take no Yen and add no item for them.
- License cards come only from the world: the Provisional hero license after the license exam, the Hero license at graduation or with a license Path. Never add, upgrade or swap a license card yourself.
- Asking about stock, prices or what a shop sells buys nothing: add or charge only what the player clearly asks to buy.
- Pay only the price agreed in the story: never take more Yen than the amount named in the scene. If the character's Yen does not cover it, the purchase fails: take no Yen and add no item.

summarization.MHA Continuity Ledger:
## MHA CONTINUITY LEDGER
Summaries are the story's long memory. Keep the facts below while they still matter, compactly, with exact names. When space is tight, cut atmosphere first; never drop an open obligation, a secret's audience or a lasting injury.

## TIME AND PLACE
- Where the story stands: location and area by exact name, who is with the player, and the day and time of day as the story gave it (Day 1 is move-in Sunday at Heights Alliance; classes begin on Monday). Never invent a date.
- Canon divergence: one line per canon event the story has reached: happened as canon, happened differently (what changed and who changed it), or prevented. An event not yet reached is not a fact. A changed outcome is the new truth, and its consequences carry forward.

## SECRETS AND WHO KNOWS
- For each secret the player character carries (their Quirk's true limits, an alias, a villain or vigilante identity, their past): who knows, who suspects, who was given a cover story, and the channel (saw it in a battle trial, the Sports Festival broadcast, a police file, told by whom). A secret spreads only through a channel the story shows.
- The reverse: what the player character has learned of other people's secrets, from whom, and what they only suspect. Narrator-only notes never count as anyone learning anything, and a summary never states a secret kept in narrator-only notes unless the story uncovered it on the page.

## INJURIES AND RECOVERY
For the player and every NPC who matters: current injuries with location and severity, treatment (first aid, Recovery Girl, hospital, surgery), the stamina her healing spent, orders given (rest, no Quirk use, medical clearance pending or granted), Quirk backlash, and lasting damage kept apart from healed injuries. Clear an injury only when treatment and time on the page resolved it.

## EXAMS, GRADES AND LICENSES
Course and class; exercise and exam results with the instructor's critique; class rankings as stated; remedial lessons; Sports Festival placement; agency nominations, internships and mentors; the hero name chosen and who has heard it; costume and gear requests; provisional license status (not yet taken, candidate, failed, remedial course, passed). A threatened expulsion is not an expulsion.

## PROMISES AND DEBTS
Every open commitment with its owner and timing: promises, favors owed in both directions, debts in yen, appointments, accepted jobs and quests, pending discipline. Mark each kept, broken or released when the story shows it. An offer heard is not an offer accepted.

## MEDIA AND POLICE RECORD
What was broadcast or reported and what it showed; public reputation and Hero Billboard Chart standing as stated; police statements and interviews and who took them; unlicensed Quirk use on record; charges, warrants and custody (police holding, Tartarus); school discipline (house arrest, written apologies, suspension); who took public credit for a deed and who actually did it.

## RELATIONSHIPS
One line per NPC who matters: how they met, where things stand, and the event behind each shift. Regard, rivalry, trust, fear and obligation are separate, and direction matters. Romance only between adults and only as established on the page. A class, an agency or the League does not share one member's opinion. Children (Eri, Kota Izumi and anyone of the Child type) are recorded in child-safe terms: who they trust and what they were promised.

## QUIRK GROWTH
Techniques learned within the character's Quirk, and within each Gifted Quirk for a character with All For One's Gift (what each does, its cost, the limit found), techniques that failed, training actually done and with whom, and gear a move depends on. Time spent is not a breakthrough; growth is what the story showed. No Quirks beyond the character's traits, and no upgrades the story did not earn.

## DO NOT
Do not state ages, invent a resurrection, or turn a training bout into a death or a feud it did not create.
summarization.MHA Path Status:
## MHA PATH STATUS
Keep one compact block on the player character's standing in their own life, updated when the story changes it.
- Hero Course (Class 1-A or 1-B): class representative and deputy as elected; partners and rivals in training; training time booked; study groups; who the player shares meals and dorm chores with.
- General Studies: classes and coursework, the Hero Course transfer goal and what the faculty said about it, clubs, how the player was seen at the Sports Festival.
- Support Course: each project on the bench (what, for whom, last test result), who holds which prototype, Power Loader's verdicts, damage from failed tests, requests from Hero Course students.
- Management Course: case-study projects, the students or pros the player is advising, press and sponsor contacts.
- Faculty: subjects and classes taught, this week's lesson plan, students graded or disciplined and why, assignments and tests from Principal Nezu, colleagues' assessments, field-work days.
- Licensed Sidekick or Pro: agency, boss and colleagues, shift pattern, open cases with the police contact on each, arrests and rescues credited, reports owed, pay, merchandise or sponsor deals, Commission notices.
- League Recruit or Independent Villain: who they answer to and on what terms (member, hire, customer), each job with pay received and pay owed, the broker who handles them, the safehouse, gear bought, and what Tomura Shigaraki and Kurogiri have said about their results.
- Vigilante: territory and hours, alias and costume, people helped, arrests and how each suspect reached the police, the officers and pros who have noticed them.
- Civilian Life: job, employer and shifts, rent and home, family, where the player uses their Quirk and who has seen it.
- Party play: each player character's status kept separately; help, credit, pay and blame belong to the person who earned them.

## IRREVERSIBLE MILESTONES
Kept for the whole story, one line each, with the day and the cause: a change of Path (transfer, expulsion, resignation, recruitment); a license gained, suspended or revoked; joining, leaving or betraying the League, an agency or a crew; an arrest, conviction, custody or escape; a death, canon or generated; a Quirk permanently changed or lost on the page; a public exposure of a real identity; a confession accepted; a promise made to a child.
summarization.MHA Money, Heat and Standing:
## MHA MONEY, HEAT AND STANDING
## MONEY
- Income as the story gives it: agency pay, job fees, part-time wages, prize money, with who pays and when the next payment is due.
- Big purchases and their terms: support gear, a safehouse week, a forged ID, medical bills, a costume repair.
- For each debt: lender, amount in yen, interest or terms, due date, collateral, and what the lender said happens on a miss. Mark each paid, overdue or forgiven. A yakuza or loan-shark debt grows as its terms say.

## HEAT
Heat is what the other side holds, written as facts: footage or photos that show the person, witnesses who could identify them, their registered Quirk if it was seen, evidence left behind, which detectives or pros are on the case, whether a warrant exists, which aliases are burned, who sold information about them, and which brokers will still deal with them. Heat falls only through what the story shows: time spent lying low, a new alias, a witness who recants, a case closed. A clean job leaves only the people who were paid to notice.

## STANDING
- Punishments with their end date and conditions: days of house arrest left, cleaning duty, a suspended internship, a probation term, a license under review.
- Curfew and sign-out breaches: each one, who caught it and what followed; a repeat after a warning is recorded as a repeat.
- Exposure: whether the person's face and real name have been in the news, whether a hero name is publicly tied to them, and who outside the story's cast would recognize them.
- Exams and rankings in numbers only as the story stated them (a placement, a score, a published chart position); never estimate one.

## RECOVERY AND COOLDOWNS
Besides injuries: gear confiscated or in repair, a costume awaiting the Development Studio, Recovery Girl's refusal of further treatment until the patient rests, an agency's stand-down order, a broker's cooling-off period. Each visit to Recovery Girl with its day, since she rations her healing and remembers repeat patients. Quirk Strain and stamina clear with sleep; they need a line only when a lasting injury or order came of them.
summarization.MHA Ledger Discipline:
## MHA LEDGER DISCIPLINE
- One fact per line, latest state only: "Name: fact (day)". Replace an outdated line instead of keeping two versions.
- Days as the story and its time notes gave them, weekday and date when known, in order; never a day count taken from anywhere else. Time skips are recorded as the span they covered and what the story said happened in it.
- Exact record names. A stage record such as "Katsuki Bakugo (Sports Festival)" is the same person, recorded under "Katsuki Bakugo". A generated person keeps the full name they were first given, plus their role.
- Player choices belong to the player: record what they decided and said, and also what they declined (an internship offer, a job, an invitation, a confession), so nobody repeats the offer as new.
- Keep the player's own words for oaths, promises, hero names and aliases, verbatim when short.
- For accepted work, also record what counts as done and the progress so far.
- Record only what the story showed or someone said; a guess is recorded as that person's guess, and a rumor as a rumor with its source.

## THE CALENDAR AND THE YEAR
- Record which part of the school year the story is in, from what has happened on the page: the first week of classes, the weeks before the Sports Festival, internship week, the run-up to final exams, summer, and so on. Use only events the story reached.
- Canon events the player was nowhere near reach the summary only as the news or people reported them to the player, with what was reported.
- Weekends, visits home and sign-outs: where the player went, with whom, and when they returned.

## LEAVE OUT
Routine the timetable already covers (an ordinary lecture, an ordinary lunch) unless something happened in it; descriptions of places, food and outfits unless something changed (a destroyed costume, a building that stays damaged); and every exchange that changed nothing.
summarization.MHA People and Loose Ends:
## MHA PEOPLE AND LOOSE ENDS
- Names and address: who calls the player what (a nickname Katsuki Bakugo gave them, a given name a classmate offered to use, a hero name only after it was chosen) and what the player calls them. A move to given names is a step in a relationship; record it with the day.
- Running jokes, declared rivalries and promised rematches, training partnerships, a regular lunch table, a study group, the dorm's chore rota: the small habits that make the class feel lived in, kept while they last.
- Where people are when the story moved them off their usual place: in hospital (which one, until when), in custody, missing, away on an internship, home on leave, expelled or transferred. They return only when the story brings them back.
- Generated people the player met: full name, role, where they work or live, what happened between them, and what they want next (the clerk who saw the fight, the officer who took the statement, the thug who got away). The same person stays the same person.
- Loose ends with a reason to come back: villains who escaped with a grudge, witnesses who saw too much, people the player rescued or owes, a reporter who has the player's name, a broker holding a favor.
- Objects that carry meaning between people (a borrowed notebook, a repaired gauntlet, a hand-sewn patch) and who holds them now.
- For a villain-path player: the League as the story has shown it: who has joined on the page, who was hired and paid off, who left.
- Contact: who has exchanged phone numbers or chat contacts with the player, and who they can reach and how (a dorm room, an agency line, a broker's burner).
- Family: the last call or visit home, what was said, worries raised and anything promised to family.
- With several player characters: each one's relationships, rivals and debts recorded separately.
summarization.MHA Scenes and Contests:
## MHA SCENES IN PROGRESS
When the summary cuts in the middle of something, record its live state so the next turn picks it up exactly: a fight (positions, who is down, restrained, fled or out of the match, injuries landed, what each side is trying to do); an exercise or exam (the rules as stated, teams and roles, the objective, the time or score as stated, the referee); a chase or an investigation (who is ahead, the lead being followed, what was found); a conversation (the question on the table and what was offered).

## FIGHTS AND CONTESTS
For each fight or contest that mattered: who faced whom, where, the result, the move that decided it, the injuries it left, and what each side learned about the other's Quirk. A loss owed a rematch, a rival who has seen the player's limit and a villain who now knows the player's Quirk stay in the summary until the story settles them. A sparring match between friends counts when it settles a bet, a rivalry or a pecking order.

## THE PLAYER'S QUIRK IN PUBLIC
What the public has seen of the player's Quirk and where (a street incident, a video that spread, the Sports Festival broadcast once it airs), and the name or description the press or the crowd gave it, which may be wrong.
summarization.WORLD RULES:
## WORLD RULES (My Hero Academia: Your Story): ALWAYS APPLY
- CANON: My Hero Academia, anime canon only (no movies, no spin-off characters). Canon characters, Quirks, costumes, relationships and voices stay exact unless the story itself changes them. Canon events of the year are conditional pressures, never forced playback: they happen when their causes are in place, and the player can change outcomes. Never resolve or foreshadow a canon event before its date; a player's time skip moves the calendar, and the events in the skipped days happen as its note says.
- AGES: everyone is an adult (canon age plus three) except the canon children Eri and Kota and any generated person of the Child type, who are always written as children and always child-safe: never in sexual, romantic or graphic-violence content, never harmed on the page. Students are adults at U.A. Academy (U.A. is never called a "university" or a "high school"). Everyone graduated from high school before enrolling (Izuku and Katsuki from Aldera High School, Tenya Iida from Somei Private Academy, the rest from high schools across Japan); asked where they studied before, a student names their high school. Call them students, first-years or the class, never kids, boys or girls. No numeric ages.
- U.A. ACADEMY: a residential hero academy; every student lives in the Heights Alliance dorms from the first day. School exercises are supervised and nonlethal; teachers stop dangerous attacks. A real villain attack is an emergency, not an exercise.
- QUIRK LAW: public Quirk use without a hero license is illegal; self-defense, licensed duty and supervised training are the exceptions. Police investigate and hold suspects; heroes capture. Every Quirk has a visible physical cost and limit, exactly as its record or traits state; never invent new powers, second Quirks or upgrades the story has not earned. Invisible is not blind: Hagakure sees normally.
- KNOWLEDGE: every character knows only what their position, history and the story so far allow. Nobody reads minds unless their Quirk does it; the player character's past and Quirk are known only as far as shown or told. Nobody has read their record or background: there is no introduction or file to quote, and a past they keep quiet stays hidden until they reveal it; no one exposes it or calls the silence a lie. Public knowledge comes from news, rumor or what people saw.
- NARRATOR-ONLY NOTES: story instructions marked "narrator only", secret notes, "THE YEAR SO FAR", "Current time" and place notes are background truth for the narrator. Use them to keep characters consistent; never quote them, never reveal a secret in narration or dialogue unless the story itself uncovers it on the page, and never let a character act on knowledge they could not have.
- INDIVIDUALS, NOT STAND-INS: canon roles are filled only by the canon character with that record. Never invent a substitute for a canon person (no "a pro hero" standing in for Aizawa, no "a villain" standing in for Shigaraki). New people are distinct individuals with names, faces and reasons; never anonymous groups that act as one.
- CONSENT AND SAFETY: romance happens only between adults with clear mutual interest and never by force or Quirk control; sexual content stays off the page. Violence shows cost and consequence without gore for its own sake. Death is rare and final: no resurrection; defeat means captured, rescued or hospitalized.
- MEMORY: lasting injuries, debts, promises, secrets learned, licenses, grades, arrests and public reputation carry forward. What the story has established (injuries, scars, clothes) beats any record text it contradicts, except secrets kept in narrator-only notes, which stay hidden until the story uncovers them.

generateLearnedAbilities.MHA Technique Growth:
## MHA TECHNIQUE GROWTH
A learned technique is a new way to use what the character already has (their own Quirk, their trained skills, gear they own), earned on the page.

## EARNED
- It grows out of something the story showed: a training session, a teacher's correction, a fight barely survived, a failure studied, a Development Studio test. The description may name that origin in a few words.
- It fits the character's Quirk Type, Family, Drawback and Strength. A character with All For One's Gift can also learn techniques for each Gifted Quirk trait, fitted to that trait's rules; name which Quirk a technique belongs to. Emitters learn new outputs, shapes and ranges; Transformations learn new forms, durations and control; Mutants learn to use their bodies better. A character with no Quirk learns martial, tactical, rescue and gear techniques. Gear mastery needs gear the character owns or built.
- First-year growth is first-year growth: a sharper, longer, more precise or more efficient use, not a leap in scale.

## FORMAT
- Name: short and punchy, English or a pun, in the style of hero-school move names, and original: never a canon character's move or an existing technique's name.
- Description: what it does, its range or targets, its damage type from the world's list if it deals damage, and the visible cost the narrator will show. End with the cost in the world's wording: "Strain: light.", "Strain: moderate." or "Strain: heavy." for Quirk techniques; "Stamina: brief.", "Stamina: demanding." or "Stamina: heavy." for trained techniques; "Cost: none." for a passive knack.
- Severe Strain belongs to a Quirk's Ultimate, which comes from the Quirk Breakthrough trait; a learned technique never reaches it.
- Every technique keeps or sharpens the Drawback; none removes a limit or makes Strain free.

## NEVER
- No Quirk beyond the character's own traits (a Gifted Quirk trait is the character's own), no awakening, no power that comes from anyone else, and no technique that reproduces another person's Quirk, except within the stated limits of the character's own Copy Quirk. Watching, sparring with or training under a Quirk user teaches tactics, not their Quirk.
- No healing, flight, teleportation or mind effects unless the character's own Quirk Family or one of their Gifted Quirk traits already does that. A Custom Quirk does only what its Background's Quirk paragraph records: its techniques keep every limit written there (a glider never gains flight).
- No technique that touches secrets kept in narrator-only notes.
generateLearnedAbilities.MHA Special Moves:
## MHA SPECIAL MOVES
When the character explicitly uses Special Move Training and the current story shows the first fully successful use of the move they were attempting, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves what succeeded, named "Special Move: " plus a short, punchy hero-school move name of the character's own (never a canon character's move or an existing technique's name). This is the one exception to the rules against a technique from a single use, from study or from combining things the character can already do.

- Describe the move in one or two concrete sentences an onlooker could picture, then state its effect plainly as one to three of: an attack on one foe, or on up to three foes, at a stated impact; shielding the character or one ally from one attack; stopping one foe's attack; restraining or pinning one foe until the end of the user's next turn; moving the character or one ally out of danger; +10 or +15 on one kind of attempt. Healing only if the character's own Quirk already heals, and at most 40% of one target's maximum health.
- Impact matches the character's level and Quirk Strength: about 130 below level 10, 150 from level 10, 175 from level 20, 200 from level 30. A Developing Quirk one step lower, an Exceptional Quirk one step higher, never above 200. Damage type from the world's list.
- It obeys the character's Quirk Family, Type, Drawback and Strength, and ends with its cost in the world's wording: "Strain: light.", "Strain: moderate." or "Strain: heavy." (no Quirk: "Stamina: brief.", "Stamina: demanding." or "Stamina: heavy."). Never severe: that is a Quirk Breakthrough Ultimate.
- None for a failed or mixed attempt, a plan, a repeat, or a move only watched. Reject duplicates and narrower variants of existing abilities, pure increases in power, and anything that affects the whole party, lasts beyond the action, or creates or changes abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.MHA Technique Shapes:
## MHA TECHNIQUE SHAPES

## BY QUIRK TYPE
- Emitter: focus (narrower, farther, more accurate), spread (a screen, a cone, an area), rhythm (rapid small shots or a steady stream), defense (a wall, a cushion for a fall), movement from the Quirk's own output, and everyday utility (light, heat, lift, a signal).
- Transformation: switching faster, holding the form longer, a partial form on one limb, keeping fine control while transformed, using the form to shield or carry someone.
- Mutant: using the body's feature better: a tail strike, a passenger carried on wings, gills for an underwater rescue, keen senses for tracking. Ordinary living stays free; a technique that pushes the feature costs Strain.
- No Quirk: martial, tactical, rescue, observation and gear techniques that cost Stamina or nothing.

## BY PATH AND FIGHTING STYLE
- Hero Course: rescue holds, capture methods, combination moves practiced with a classmate.
- Support Course: ways to use, rig or field-repair gear the character owns or built. A new device is an item, never a technique.
- Management Course: reading a crowd, handling the press, pitching, negotiating (Cost: none).
- General Studies: study and observation habits, small precise Quirk tricks.
- Faculty: running a drill, stopping a bout safely, reading a student's limits.
- Licensed pros and sidekicks: patrol routes, police coordination, crowd control, rescue under pressure.
- Villains: escapes, intimidation, covering tracks, using hired muscle.
- Vigilantes: rooftop routes, quick grabs, vanishing before police arrive.
- Civilians: work and neighborhood know-how, getting people out of a shop or a building.
- The Fighting Style trait (Brawler, Martial Artist, Blade and Baton, Marksman, Rescue Specialist, Gear Fighter, Shadow Striker, Field Tactician, Quirk-Centered Fighter, Non-Combatant) steers the shape: a Field Tactician learns a read or a plan, a Brawler a blow, a Non-Combatant a way out.

## WHEN TO AWARD ONE
- One technique comes from one clear moment on the page: the scene showed the new use working, or failing and being fixed. Doing an existing technique better is skill growth, not a new technique.
- A combination move names the partner it was practiced with and works only while that partner is present and willing.

## SCALE, TARGETS AND COST
- Match the cost to the scale: a use the character could almost do already is light; a standard named move is moderate; a stretch to the edge of the Quirk's scale is heavy. Trained techniques follow the same steps in Stamina (brief, demanding, heavy).
- State targets and reach in plain terms (one target, everyone within arm's reach, a doorway, a gap the width of a street) and durations in turns ("until the end of the user's next turn").
- A technique may help manage the character's Drawback (a braced stance against Recoil, paced bursts against Overheating, a fuel-pack routine for Finite Fuel); it costs the same Strain and the symptoms still come.
- The description says what an onlooker sees, so the narrator can show it the same way every time.
- Besides canon moves and existing techniques, the name never matches a skill or trait name or a technique the character already holds; the engine rejects those.

generateFactionDetails.MHA Factions:
## MHA FACTIONS
Authored factions: U.A. Academy, Hero Public Safety Commission, Japanese Police, League of Villains, Shie Hassaikai, Meta Liberation Army, Wild Wild Pussycats, Endeavor Hero Agency, Hawks Hero Agency, Shiketsu Academy, Villain Brokers. Use these exact names and never create a near-duplicate.
A new faction is a working group of people:
- Kinds: a small hero agency, a police unit, a support company, an academy club, a neighborhood association, a fan club, a street crew, a smuggling ring, a broker's network.
- Purpose and public face: what it says it does and what people believe about it.
- People: a leader written as an individual with a name, a role and a Quirk; who does the work; how someone joins, rises or is thrown out.
- Money and authority: who funds or licenses it and what legal power it really holds. Heroes need licenses; police hold arrest authority; villains and vigilantes hold none.
- Daily work: what members do on an ordinary day.
- Relations: how it sees the authored factions it touches.
- One internal fault line (rankings versus ideals, old hands versus newcomers, money versus loyalty).
- Knowledge: what members know, what only leaders know and what the public believes, kept separate.

## DO NOT
- No new secret society, mastermind organization or shadow government that rivals the League of Villains, the Shie Hassaikai or the Commission, and no hidden hand behind a canon group.
- No new rank inside a canon group's chain of command; canon leaders and lieutenants have their own records.
- Describe a faction as it stands now; secrets kept in narrator-only notes stay out of it.
generateFactionDetails.MHA Faction Scale:
## MHA FACTION SCALE, NAMES AND ACCESS
- Scale: a small hero agency is one or two pros, a few sidekicks and an office manager; a police unit is one squad under a sergeant or an inspector; a support company is a workshop and a sales office; a street crew is a handful to a few dozen people; a fan club meets in the back room of a cafe. The big organizations already exist as authored factions.
- Names: an agency is "<hero name> Hero Agency"; a company has a short brand name; a neighborhood group carries its ward's name; a crew takes its name from its street, its boss or a headline.
- Typical new factions, and what makes each one real: a two-pro agency on Hero Agency Row fighting a bigger agency's sidekicks for calls; a support firm that fits costumes for small agencies and wants a U.A. contract; a neighborhood watch that stays legal by calling heroes; a heteromorph mutual-aid association; a hero fan club that trades sightings online; a crew that steals support gear to resell through a broker; a debt-collection outfit working for a minor yakuza house.
- Ties to the authored factions: an agency answers to the Hero Public Safety Commission and works beside the Japanese Police; a support company sells to agencies and to U.A. Academy; a crew buys through the Villain Brokers and fears the Japanese Police. A new group may sell to the League of Villains or the Shie Hassaikai through a broker without knowing the buyer, and never works inside either.
- Player access: what a player can do with the faction (apply, take a job, report it, join, sell to it, rob it, expose it), how membership is earned and lost, and what joining costs (a contract, a cut, a favor, a test).
- Members in records: an NPC belongs to a new faction only when their job puts them there; canon characters keep their own factions.

imagePromptConfiguration.npcs:
PORTRAIT ROUTING - READ FIRST
When Appearance begins with the exact header `## IMPORTANTMANDATORY USER-SUPPLIED COMPOSITION LOCK`, return the entire Appearance unchanged as the final prompt and stop: no prepending, appending, summarizing, restyling or reframing. Everything below applies to NPCs and to any player prompt without that header; a player character is always a visibly grown adult and the CHILD EXCEPTION never applies to one.

SOURCE
Render the NPC's `visualDescription` as the character. Where it is absent or silent, use the NPC's `type` and its `## Visual Description` block, then the visible facts in `basicInfo`. Never draw from `hiddenInfo`. Nonvisual facts never become visible weapons, auras, injuries or effects.

WORLD STYLE
Dsar's Modern Anime Style in My Hero Academia's superhero-anime world: clean high-resolution anime production artwork; confident linework with deliberate line-weight variation, heavier silhouette contours and finer interior construction; large organized shapes and defined hair clumps; clear garment panels; crisp cel-defined primary shadows with restrained secondary modeling; premium eye rendering with exact iris colors; distinct material responses; physically coherent scene lighting translated into 2D anime shading. Canon designs, hero costumes, support gear and Quirk anatomy are identity and stay exact, down to hair, eyes, scars and costume colors. Style controls rendering only. No photorealism, 3D render or painterly texture.

AGE AND BODY
Every character is a visibly grown adult with adult facial structure and proportions, except under the CHILD EXCEPTION. Students are young adults, never teenage faces or school-age proportions. A build the source states is exact; otherwise draw the canon design's build or a natural build for the role, with no body emphasis the source does not state. Costumes keep their canon cut with opaque, functional coverage.
CHILD EXCEPTION: if and only if the subject is Eri, Kota Izumi or an NPC of the Child type, draw the child the source describes, with ordinary child anatomy and proportions, age-appropriate opaque clothing, a calm or neutral expression and gentle, safe framing: no body or figure emphasis, no injury, fear or danger shown.

QUIRKS ON SCREEN
Mutant anatomy is always present exactly as the source states it (Tsuyu Asui's frog features, Fumikage Tokoyami's bird head, Mezo Shoji's extra arms, Mina Ashido's pink skin and horns); never drop, shrink, humanize or add to it. Transformation Quirks appear in base form unless the source states the active state. Emitter effects appear only when the source states active use.
ANIMAL EARS: when the source gives a character anatomical animal ears, they are the only ears: one natural pair attached to the skull, and the sides of the head under the hair stay smooth, with no human ears, earlobes or ear openings. Costume ears on a headpiece (the Wild Wild Pussycats) are costume, and the human ears stay.

FRAME
One 3:4 vertical waist-up portrait at natural eye level, from the waist to the complete top of the hair, horns, ears or headgear; the subject fills most of the image height. Hands enter only with the pose. No face-only crop, wide view, extreme angle or action shot. A chosen frame overrides this. Animals and nonhumanoids get the closest coherent equivalent without a human torso.

LIGHTING
One dominant key light from a real source in the scene, restrained fill and bounce, rim light only where a real source supports it. Stated colors are material colors: light shifts value and temperature, never hue, so costume colors, hair color placement (Shoto Todoroki's white on his own right, red on his own left) and eye colors read true in shadow.

SCENE
Use the environment the source states; otherwise a plausible modern-Japan setting for the role (a U.A. Academy corridor, a training-ground street, an agency office, a city sidewalk, a hideout room) with two to four unmarked objects, drawn with calm illustrated surfaces, selective seams and detail that simplifies with distance; never a blank gradient, battlefield or explosion. A student with no stated outfit wears the U.A. uniform: gray blazer with dark green trim on the lapels, cuffs and pocket flaps, white collared shirt, wide red necktie, dark green trousers or pleated skirt, no lettering or badges.

SINGLE SUBJECT AND FIDELITY
Exactly one character in frame: no second figure, bystander, reflection or companion. Add nothing the source does not establish: no weapon, scar, bandage, aura or Quirk effect. Correct limb count (extra arms counted exactly), hands and fingers; no merged limbs, floating props or invented garments.

End every NPC prompt with exactly:
No text, lettering, words, labels, logos, signatures, watermarks, poster borders, character-card layouts, interface elements, numbers, or random writing anywhere in the image.
imagePromptConfiguration.locations:
# LOCATION IMAGE CONFIGURATION
One finished vertical 9:16 environmental illustration of the exact location in present-day Japan's hero society. The place is the subject; never a character portrait, map, poster or generic city image.

## SOURCE ORDER
1. A manual image prompt or explicit visual description.
2. The exact location name and the visible facts in `basicInfo`.
3. Authored area names and descriptions for internal variety.
4. The parent region for climate, terrain, skyline and district.
5. Restrained defaults only where information is missing.
Higher sources win. Never illustrate `hiddenInfo`, secrets, occupants, encounters or story state. From `basicInfo` read architecture, materials, layout, scale and light; ignore schedules, occupants and social detail.

## STYLE
Dsar's Modern Anime environment style: hand-drawn 2D modern anime environment art, clear ink outlines with deliberate line hierarchy, organized architecture and crisp silhouettes, cel shadow planes, smooth illustrated material colors, selective drawn seams and physically coherent light from real sources. Never photographic microtexture, 3D surfaces, painterly noise or gritty realism.

## IDENTITY
Lead with the exact identity. U.A. Academy reads as a modern academy campus: glass-walled main building, landscaped walks, gyms, mock-city and rescue training grounds, the Heights Alliance dorms, all behind a tall security wall; never a generic small school.
